questions.stem: The training programme lasts \_\_\_ six weeks, and it should be finished \_\_\_ the middle of March.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** "for + a length of time" states duration (for six weeks); "by + a point in time" states a deadline the finishing must not pass (by the middle of March).

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) "since six weeks" treats a length as a start point (misconception: since = for, from Hindi 'se'); "until March" wrongly says the programme continues up to March. (c) "during" needs an event noun, not a measured length (during/for confusion). (d) "finished until March" says the finishing keeps happening up to March; a completed action needs by, not until.

**Principle:** for measures how long; by marks a deadline; until marks a state continuing up to a point; during locates an action inside a named period.

**Memory tip:** "by" is a finish line; "until" is the road running up to that line.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Prepositions of Time

questions.stem: Guests may stay in the hall \_\_\_ ten o'clock, but the doors must be locked \_\_\_ then.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** "stay until ten" is a continuing state that lasts up to a point; "locked by ten" is a single completed action with a deadline.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) reversed: "stay by ten" is wrong because staying is continuous; "locked until ten" means it stays locked up to ten. (c) "stay for ten o'clock" wrongly uses for with a clock time instead of a length. (d) "locked until ten" again gives the wrong meaning.

**Principle:** Continuing states take until; one-off completions take by.

**Memory tip:** You wait until a time; you deliver by a time.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Prepositions of Time

questions.stem: Assembly starts \_\_\_ 8:15 \_\_\_ Monday morning, right \_\_\_ the start of the new term.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** at + clock time (8:15); on + a specific day (Monday morning is a named day, so on, not in); at the start is a fixed phrase.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b)/(c)/(d) permute the rules wrongly: "on 8:15", "in 8:15" and "in Monday morning" all break the pattern. The common trap is using "in the morning" logic for "on Monday morning" (a specific day forces on).

**Principle:** at a point in the clock; on a day; in a span such as a month or year.

**Memory tip:** at a time, on a day, in a bigger span.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Prepositions of Time

questions.stem: Our science teacher has guided this club \_\_\_ 2021, so she has led it \_\_\_ about five years.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** since + the point where something began (2021), used with the present perfect; for + the length of time (five years).

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) swaps them ("for 2021" and "since five years" are both wrong). (c) "from 2021" needs an end point (from 2021 to now); with a still-continuing period the correct word is since. (d) "for ... from" is nonsense here.

**Principle:** since marks the beginning of a still-continuing period; for measures its length.

**Memory tip:** since points back to a moment; for measures the stretch.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Prepositions of Time

questions.stem: The 9:00 train left exactly \_\_\_; fortunately we arrived \_\_\_ to jump aboard.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** on time = punctual, exactly as scheduled (the train left at 9:00); in time (to do something) = early enough, with time to spare.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) a train leaving "exactly in time" is wrong; leaving as scheduled is on time. (c)/(d) repeat one phrase and lose the contrast: "arrived on time to jump aboard" drops the 'with enough time' sense that in time carries.

**Principle:** on time = according to the schedule; in time (for/to) = soon enough.

**Memory tip:** on time = the clock agrees; in time = you made it before the door shut.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Prepositions of Time

fields.Cognitive skill: Fixed time phrases: on time vs in time

questions.stem: Explain the difference in meaning between: (i) 'The report will be ready in an hour.' (ii) 'The report will be ready within an hour.'
questions.answer: (i) in an hour = after a full hour has passed / it takes about an hour, so the natural reading is 'ready at the end of roughly sixty minutes'. (ii) within an hour = at some point before an hour passes - any time up to sixty minutes, possibly much sooner; 'within' stresses the outer limit.
questions.solution:
**Answer:** (i) in an hour = after a full hour has passed / it takes about an hour, so the natural reading is 'ready at the end of roughly sixty minutes'. (ii) within an hour = at some point before an hour passes - any time up to sixty minutes, possibly much sooner; 'within' stresses the outer limit.

**Why the other options are wrong:** The usual error is treating them as identical. The point missed is that 'in + period' lands on the end of the period, while 'within + period' allows anything up to that end.

**Principle:** in + time = at the end of that span; within + time = at or before the end of that span.

**Memory tip:** 'in' lands on the hour mark; 'within' lands anywhere inside the hour.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Prepositions of Time

questions.stem: The rehearsals were messy, but \_\_\_ the play was a hit; the cast bowed \_\_\_ the last scene.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** in the end = finally, as the eventual outcome after a process; at the end (of something) = at the final point of a thing (the last scene).

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) swapped: "at the end the play was a hit" reads as a point in time, not an outcome, and "bowed in the end of the last scene" is wrong. (c)/(d) repeat one phrase and so mismatch one meaning. Trap: assuming the two phrases are interchangeable.

**Principle:** in the end = the final result after everything; at the end (of X) = the final point of X.

**Memory tip:** in the end = 'after all that'; at the end = 'the tail of it'.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Prepositions of Time

questions.stem: You should reach the exam hall \_\_\_ the bell rings; aim to be seated \_\_\_ 9:30 at the latest.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** before + an event/clause ('before the bell rings'); by + a clock time as a deadline, which pairs naturally with 'at the latest'.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) "by the bell rings" is wrong because by cannot take a clause (you would need 'by the time'); 'seated before 9:30 at the latest' clashes with the deadline sense. (c) "reach until the bell" is wrong. (d) "seated until 9:30" means staying seated up to 9:30 - wrong meaning.

**Principle:** before + a clause or event; by + a deadline point (often with 'at the latest').

**Memory tip:** before = earlier than that moment; by = no later than that moment.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Prepositions of Time

questions.stem: My grandfather has collected stamps \_\_\_ 1998.
questions.solution:
**Answer:** since

**Explanation:** The present perfect ('has collected') with a start point (a year) takes since.

**Why the other options are wrong:** 'for 1998' treats a point as a length (since/for confusion); 'from 1998' needs an end point, e.g. 'from 1998 to 2005'.

**Principle:** since marks the beginning of a period that is still going on.

**Memory tip:** since = 'starting from that year and still going'.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Prepositions of Time

questions.stem: \_\_\_ the thunderstorm the lights flickered, and the power stayed off \_\_\_ two hours.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** during + a named event (the thunderstorm); for + a measured length of time (two hours).

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) "For the thunderstorm the lights flickered" changes the meaning of for to purpose; "off during two hours" wrongly uses during with a length. (c) "Since the thunderstorm" means 'ever since', changing the meaning. (d) "off since two hours" is wrong.

**Principle:** during answers 'inside which event?'; for answers 'how long?'.

**Memory tip:** during locates you inside an event; for measures the clock.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Prepositions of Time

questions.stem: Correct the preposition error: 'She has been living in Pune since three years.'
questions.answer: 'since three years' should be 'for three years': 'She has been living in Pune for three years.'
questions.solution:
**Answer:** 'since three years' should be 'for three years': 'She has been living in Pune for three years.'

**Why the other options are wrong:** Keeping since is the classic error (Hindi/regional 'se' covers both since and for). since needs a start point (since 2021), not a duration.

**Principle:** since + a point in time; for + a duration.

**Memory tip:** If you can answer 'how long?', use for.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Prepositions of Time

questions.stem: In the sentence 'We stayed with our cousins \_\_\_ the summer holidays', are both 'over' and 'during' acceptable? Justify briefly.
questions.answer: Yes - both are acceptable and mean roughly the same (at some time in, or throughout, the holidays). 'over' is a little more informal and stresses spanning the whole stretch; 'during' is neutral and simply places the stay inside that period.
questions.solution:
**Answer:** Yes - both are acceptable and mean roughly the same (at some time in, or throughout, the holidays). 'over' is a little more informal and stresses spanning the whole stretch; 'during' is neutral and simply places the stay inside that period.

**Why the other options are wrong:** Errors: assuming only one can be correct; or reading 'over' here as 'above'. Over and during both have a 'in the course of a period' meaning.

**Principle:** over and during can both mean 'in the course of' a period; the difference is register/emphasis, not grammar.

**Memory tip:** over = across the whole span; during = somewhere inside the span - usually interchangeable for holidays.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Prepositions of Time

questions.stem: We reached the campsite \_\_\_ night and set off again \_\_\_ dawn.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** at night and at dawn are fixed: night, dawn, noon and midnight are treated as points and take at (unlike 'in the morning/evening').

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b)/(d) "in night" is wrong; (c) "in dawn" is wrong. Trap: applying the 'in the morning' pattern to night/dawn.

**Principle:** at night, at dawn, at noon, at midnight (points); but in the morning/afternoon/evening.

**Memory tip:** night, noon, dawn, midnight are pinpoints - use at.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Prepositions of Time

questions.stem: Rewrite using 'by': 'You must return the equipment no later than Friday.'
questions.answer: 'You must return the equipment by Friday.'
questions.solution:
**Answer:** 'You must return the equipment by Friday.'

**Why the other options are wrong:** Using until ('return until Friday') changes it into a continuous action; till has the same problem. 'No later than' is exactly the deadline meaning of by.

**Principle:** by expresses a deadline = 'not later than'.

**Memory tip:** 'no later than' is just a long way of saying by.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Prepositions of Time

questions.stem: The shop is busiest \_\_\_ 12 \_\_\_ 2 in the afternoon.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** between ... and ... is the correct correlative pair for a span between two times.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) mixes pairs: from goes with to, not and. (c) mixes pairs: between goes with and, not to. (d) 'since 12' needs a present-perfect start point. Trap: crossing the two fixed pairs.

**Principle:** between ... and ...; from ... to ... - never cross the pairs.

**Memory tip:** between marries and; from marries to.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Prepositions of Time

questions.stem: Don't worry - the results will be announced \_\_\_ a few days.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** in + a future period = at the end of that period counting from now ('in a few days' = a few days from now).

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) since needs a past start point. (c) for gives a duration, the wrong meaning. (d) by needs a definite point ('by Friday'), not a vague length. Trap: using for or by for 'a few days from now'.

**Principle:** in + period (future) = at the end of that period from now.

**Memory tip:** 'in a few days' = a few days from now.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Prepositions of Time

questions.stem: Explain why 'I will wait for you until 6' is correct but 'I will wait for you by 6' is not.
questions.answer: Waiting is a continuous action that lasts up to a point, so it needs until (up to 6). by marks the deadline for a single completed action ('finish by 6', 'arrive by 6'). You cannot 'wait by 6' because waiting is not a one-moment event.
questions.solution:
**Answer:** Waiting is a continuous action that lasts up to a point, so it needs until (up to 6). by marks the deadline for a single completed action ('finish by 6', 'arrive by 6'). You cannot 'wait by 6' because waiting is not a one-moment event.

**Why the other options are wrong:** Error: treating by and until as interchangeable. The verb's type decides the choice.

**Principle:** until = a state lasting up to a point (ongoing actions); by = a deadline for a completed action.

**Memory tip:** Ongoing action -\> until. One-and-done action -\> by.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Prepositions of Time

questions.stem: India became a republic \_\_\_ 26 January \_\_\_ 1950.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** on + a specific date (26 January); in + a year (1950).

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) "in 26 January" is wrong; (c) "at 26 January" is wrong; (d) "at 1950" is wrong. Trap: mismatching date and year rules.

**Principle:** on + a specific date; in + a year.

**Memory tip:** on the day, in the year.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Prepositions of Time

questions.stem: Complete B's reply with the correct time prepositions. A: When is the school trip? B: It's \_\_\_ the 14th, and we'll be away \_\_\_ three days.
questions.solution:
**Answer:** on (the 14th) ... for (three days).

**Why the other options are wrong:** 'in the 14th' or 'at the 14th' is wrong (dates take on); 'since three days' or 'during three days' is wrong (a duration takes for).

**Principle:** on + a date; for + a duration.

**Memory tip:** on a date, for a stretch.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Prepositions of Time

questions.stem: The mangoes ripen \_\_\_ summer, usually \_\_\_ May or June.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** in + a season (summer); in + a month (May/June).

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) "at summer" is wrong; (c) "on summer" is wrong; (d) "on June" is wrong. Trap: using at/on for large spans.

**Principle:** in + seasons, months and years (big spans of time).

**Memory tip:** big spans of time -\> in.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Prepositions of Time

questions.stem: Which is correct and why is the other wrong: (i) 'I finished the essay in two hours.' (ii) 'I finished the essay for two hours.'
questions.answer: (i) is correct: in two hours = the task took two hours to complete. (ii) is wrong: for two hours describes how long a continuing action lasted, but 'finish' is a single completed moment. (Note 'I wrote the essay for two hours' is fine, because writing is ongoing.)
questions.solution:
**Answer:** (i) is correct: in two hours = the task took two hours to complete. (ii) is wrong: for two hours describes how long a continuing action lasted, but 'finish' is a single completed moment. (Note 'I wrote the essay for two hours' is fine, because writing is ongoing.)

**Why the other options are wrong:** Error: assuming for always marks a length of time regardless of the verb. Completion verbs (finish, arrive) do not take for + duration.

**Principle:** for + duration suits continuing actions; completion verbs take in for the time taken.

**Memory tip:** You do something for a while, but you complete it in a certain time.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Prepositions of Time

questions.stem: \_\_\_ the age of ten she had already written a novel; she published it \_\_\_ 2020.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** at the age of ... (age is treated as a point); in + a year (2020).

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) "In the age of ten" is wrong; (c) "On the age" is wrong; (d) "on 2020" is wrong. Trap: mismatching 'at the age of' and 'in + year'.

**Principle:** at the age of ...; in + year.

**Memory tip:** 'at' pins a point (an age); 'in' holds a year.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Prepositions of Time

fields.Cognitive skill: at with points, in with years

questions.stem: He hasn't spoken to me \_\_\_ we quarrelled, which is now \_\_\_ almost a month.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** since + a past-event clause ('since we quarrelled'), used with the present perfect; for + the length of time (almost a month).

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) swaps them. (c) "from we quarrelled" is wrong because from does not take this clause; since is required. (d) "for ... from" is nonsense here.

**Principle:** since can introduce a clause marking when something began; for gives the length.

**Memory tip:** since = 'starting when X happened'; for = 'lasting this long'.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Prepositions of Time

questions.stem: Correct the time prepositions: 'The meeting is scheduled at Tuesday in 3 p.m.'
questions.answer: 'on Tuesday at 3 p.m.': 'The meeting is scheduled on Tuesday at 3 p.m.'
questions.solution:
**Answer:** 'on Tuesday at 3 p.m.': 'The meeting is scheduled on Tuesday at 3 p.m.'

**Why the other options are wrong:** 'at Tuesday' is wrong (days take on); 'in 3 p.m.' is wrong (clock times take at). Trap: swapping the in/on/at rules.

**Principle:** on + a day; at + a clock time.

**Memory tip:** on the day, at the time.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Prepositions of Time

questions.stem: She waited \_\_\_ the bus stop, \_\_\_ front of the bakery.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** at + a specific point/location (the bus stop); 'in front of' is a fixed phrase.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) "in the bus stop" is wrong - you wait at a stop. (c) "on front of" is not a phrase. (d) "on the bus stop" is wrong. Trap: breaking the fixed phrase 'in front of'.

**Principle:** at for a specific point/location; 'in front of' is one unbreakable unit.

**Memory tip:** at pins you to a spot; 'in front of' is a single locked phrase.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Place and Position

fields.Cognitive skill: at for a point + fixed phrase

questions.stem: We arrived \_\_\_ the cinema early and found our seats \_\_\_ row H.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** arrive at + a building/place (the cinema); in + a row (seats are in a row).

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b)/(d) 'arrive in the cinema' is wrong - arrive in is for towns/countries, arrive at for buildings. (b) 'seats at row H' and (c) 'seats on row H' are wrong; rows take in.

**Principle:** arrive at + a building/place; arrive in + a town/country; in + a row.

**Memory tip:** You arrive at a building but in a city; you sit in a row.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Place and Position

questions.stem: She gently pulled a blanket \_\_\_ the sleeping baby.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** over can mean covering or spanning a surface; a blanket covers the baby, so over.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) above = at a higher level with no contact/covering - wrong, a blanket covers. (c) 'on top' needs 'of' ('on top of'). (d) 'upon' = on/onto and gives the wrong picture. Trap: confusing 'higher than' (above) with 'covering' (over).

**Principle:** over = covering or spanning a surface; above = simply higher up.

**Memory tip:** A blanket goes over you (covering); a lamp hangs above you (higher up).
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Place and Position

questions.stem: Explain the difference: (i) 'The helicopter hovered above the stadium.' (ii) 'The helicopter flew over the stadium.'
questions.answer: (i) above = at a higher position, staying put (a vertical relationship, often static). (ii) over = crossing/passing across the top of it (movement across, or covering the whole area). 'Above' says it is higher; 'over' says it passed across or spans it.
questions.solution:
**Answer:** (i) above = at a higher position, staying put (a vertical relationship, often static). (ii) over = crossing/passing across the top of it (movement across, or covering the whole area). 'Above' says it is higher; 'over' says it passed across or spans it.

**Why the other options are wrong:** Error: treating them as identical; forgetting that over often implies crossing or covering.

**Principle:** above = higher level (position); over = across the top / covering (often movement).

**Memory tip:** above = simply higher; over = across or on top of.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Place and Position

questions.stem: By midnight the temperature had dropped \_\_\_ zero, and it stayed \_\_\_ freezing all night.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** below zero / below freezing: points on a scale (temperature, marks, sea level) take below, not under.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b)/(c)/(d) use under for scale values, which is wrong; under is for a physical position beneath something, not for a level on a scale.

**Principle:** Use below (not under) for measurements/levels on a scale.

**Memory tip:** On a scale - temperature, marks, sea level - it's below, not under.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Place and Position

questions.stem: \_\_\_ his textbooks, he keeps a dictionary \_\_\_ his desk.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** Besides = in addition to (his textbooks); beside = next to (his desk).

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) swapped: 'Beside his textbooks' means physically next to them, and 'a dictionary besides his desk' is wrong. (c)/(d) repeat one word and mismatch a meaning. Trap: the single letter 's' flips the meaning.

**Principle:** beside = next to (position); besides = in addition to / apart from.

**Memory tip:** The extra 's' in besides means 'something extra'.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Place and Position

questions.stem: The secret was shared \_\_\_ the three founders and never spread \_\_\_ the wider staff.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** between the three founders: they are distinct, individually linked parties, so between works even for three; among the wider staff: an undifferentiated group/mass.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) swapped: 'among the three founders' hides their individual link, and 'spread between the wider staff' wrongly treats a mass as separate parties. (c)/(d) ignore the distinction. Trap: the myth that between is only for two.

**Principle:** between = individually distinct parties (even several); among = an undivided group/mass.

**Memory tip:** between = named individuals linked to each other; among = a crowd.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Place and Position

questions.stem: A student says, 'between can only be used for two things.' Give one correct sentence that shows this rule is too simple, and explain.
questions.answer: Example: 'There is close cooperation between France, Germany and Italy.' Here between links three countries because they are treated as separate parties with links to one another. between is used whenever items are seen as distinct individuals; among is for an undivided group. So 'two only' is an oversimplification.
questions.solution:
**Answer:** Example: 'There is close cooperation between France, Germany and Italy.' Here between links three countries because they are treated as separate parties with links to one another. between is used whenever items are seen as distinct individuals; among is for an undivided group. So 'two only' is an oversimplification.

**Why the other options are wrong:** Error: the memorised 'two = between, three or more = among' rule. Number is not the deciding factor.

**Principle:** The deciding factor is distinctness of the parties, not how many there are.

**Memory tip:** If you can picture the items as separate points linked to each other, use between - however many there are.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Place and Position

fields.Task type: Explain the error in the rule

questions.stem: He isn't \_\_\_ home right now; he's still \_\_\_ work.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** at home / at work / at school are fixed location phrases with at.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) "in home" is wrong; (c) 'in work' (BrE colloquial 'in work' = employed) is not the intended 'at the workplace' meaning and is misleading; (d) both wrong. Trap: using in for these fixed phrases.

**Principle:** at home / at work / at school are fixed phrases.

**Memory tip:** These three go with at, not in.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Place and Position

questions.stem: The bakery is \_\_\_ the library - you see it right across the road as you leave the library steps.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** opposite = directly facing, on the other side, across from.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'in front of' = ahead of / on the front side, not across the road - it confuses 'facing across' with 'ahead of'. (c) 'before' is mainly time/order, not physical facing. (d) 'beside' = next to, not across.

**Principle:** opposite = directly facing / on the other side; in front of = ahead of / on the front side.

**Memory tip:** opposite = face to face across a gap; in front of = standing before it on the same side.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Place and Position

questions.stem: Explain the difference: (i) 'The taxi stopped in front of the hotel.' (ii) 'The taxi stopped opposite the hotel.'
questions.answer: (i) in front of the hotel = right before its entrance, on the hotel's own side of the road. (ii) opposite the hotel = across the street, facing it. So (i) is at the hotel's door; (ii) is on the far side of the road.
questions.solution:
**Answer:** (i) in front of the hotel = right before its entrance, on the hotel's own side of the road. (ii) opposite the hotel = across the street, facing it. So (i) is at the hotel's door; (ii) is on the far side of the road.

**Why the other options are wrong:** Error: assuming both describe the same spot.

**Principle:** in front of = directly before (same side); opposite = across from (other side).

**Memory tip:** in front of = at its face; opposite = across from its face.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Place and Position

questions.stem: The manager is \_\_\_ the office today, so email her instead; her assistant is waiting \_\_\_ the meeting room for you.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** out of the office = away / not present; outside the meeting room = positioned just beyond it.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'outside the office today' means physically just beyond the building, not the intended 'away/unavailable'; 'waiting out of the meeting room' is wrong (out of = motion/absence). (c)/(d) repeat and mismatch a meaning.

**Principle:** out of = away from / not in a state (motion or absence); outside = positioned beyond something (static).

**Memory tip:** out of = not in it (gone/away); outside = standing just beyond it.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Place and Position

questions.stem: There's a decent chemist \_\_\_ the station, roughly five minutes' walk from the platforms.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** near = in the general vicinity, not touching; a five-minute walk fits near.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) next to = immediately adjacent - contradicts 'five minutes away'. (c) beside = right alongside - same problem. (d) by = right beside/very close - contradicts the distance.

**Principle:** near = in the general vicinity; next to / beside / by = immediately adjacent.

**Memory tip:** next to means touching-close; near means 'around there'.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Place and Position

questions.stem: There were hundreds of people \_\_\_ the concert, all packed \_\_\_ the open-air arena.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** at + an event (the concert); in + an enclosed space (the arena).

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'in the concert' is odd (you attend at an event) and 'packed at the arena' is wrong. (c) 'packed at the arena' is wrong. (d) 'on the concert' is wrong.

**Principle:** at + an event; in + an enclosed space.

**Memory tip:** at the event, in the enclosure.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Place and Position

questions.stem: Correct the preposition: 'The teacher wrote the date in the top of the whiteboard.'
questions.answer: 'in the top' should be 'at the top': 'The teacher wrote the date at the top of the whiteboard.'
questions.solution:
**Answer:** 'in the top' should be 'at the top': 'The teacher wrote the date at the top of the whiteboard.'

**Why the other options are wrong:** Using in for a position on a surface is the error; 'at the top / at the bottom' is the fixed phrase for positions on a page or board.

**Principle:** at the top / at the bottom for positions on a surface.

**Memory tip:** top and bottom of a page or board take at.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Place and Position

questions.stem: The old mill stands \_\_\_ the Thames, and a footbridge crosses \_\_\_ the river just beside it.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** A building/settlement 'stands on' a river (e.g. 'a town on the Ganges'); a bridge goes over the water.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'in the Thames' = inside the water, wrong. (c) 'at the Thames' is not idiomatic for 'situated on a river'. (d) 'crosses on the river' is wrong; bridges go over.

**Principle:** Settlements sit on a river; bridges go over water.

**Memory tip:** 'Stratford-on-Avon' - places are on their river; bridges arch over.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Place and Position

questions.stem: They live \_\_\_ 42 Park Lane, \_\_\_ the second floor.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** at + a specific house number/address (42 Park Lane); on + a floor (the second floor).

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'in 42 Park Lane' and 'at the second floor' are wrong. (c) 'on 42' and 'in the second floor' are wrong. (d) 'in the second floor' is wrong.

**Principle:** at + a specific address/number; on + a floor.

**Memory tip:** at the exact number, on the floor.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Place and Position

questions.stem: By the time I was sitting \_\_\_ my car, the other students were already \_\_\_ the school bus.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** You sit in a car/taxi, but you are on a bus/train/plane/ship.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) swapped: 'on my car' means on the roof, and 'in the school bus' is not the idiom. (c) 'in the school bus' is less idiomatic than on. (d) 'on my car' = on top.

**Principle:** You sit in a small private vehicle (car/taxi) but on a large public one (bus/train/plane).

**Memory tip:** Small private vehicle -\> in; large public vehicle you can walk about in -\> on.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Place and Position

questions.stem: Rewrite using 'in front of': 'A tall man was standing before me and blocked my view.'
questions.answer: 'A tall man was standing in front of me and blocked my view.'
questions.solution:
**Answer:** 'A tall man was standing in front of me and blocked my view.'

**Why the other options are wrong:** Thinking before is only about time is the error; here it means position, so 'in front of' fits.

**Principle:** before can mean 'in front of' (position) as well as 'earlier than' (time).

**Memory tip:** 'standing before the judge' = standing in front of the judge.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Place and Position

questions.stem: Find and correct the wrong place preposition: 'Meet me on the entrance of the mall at noon.'
questions.answer: 'on the entrance' should be 'at the entrance': 'Meet me at the entrance of the mall at noon.'
questions.solution:
**Answer:** 'on the entrance' should be 'at the entrance': 'Meet me at the entrance of the mall at noon.'

**Why the other options are wrong:** Using on for a meeting point is the error; at is used for meeting points and specific spots.

**Principle:** at + a meeting point / specific location (at the entrance, at the gate, at the corner).

**Memory tip:** Meeting spots take at.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Place and Position

questions.stem: Choose the best option for this notice: 'Cycles must not be parked \_\_\_ the fire exit or left \_\_\_ the stairwell.'
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** in front of the fire exit = blocking its front, outside it; in the stairwell = inside the stairwell.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'in the front of the fire exit' means the front part inside it (in front of vs in the front of), and 'on the stairwell' is wrong. (c) 'before the fire exit' is ambiguous/time-like and 'at the stairwell' is a point, not 'inside'. (d) 'at the stairwell' is a point, not 'inside'.

**Principle:** in front of (outside, facing) is not the same as in the front of (the front area inside); in + an enclosed space.

**Memory tip:** in front of = outside its face; in the front of = the front part inside it.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Place and Position

fields.Cognitive skill: in front of vs in the front of

questions.stem: The lorry skidded and crashed \_\_\_ the barrier; luckily the driver was still safely \_\_\_ his seat.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** crash into = movement ending in impact (into); 'in his seat' = a static position.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'crashed in the barrier' loses the impact-movement, and 'into his seat' wrongly suggests motion for a driver sitting still. (c) 'into his seat' is wrong. (d) 'crashed in the barrier' is wrong. Trap: using 'in' after a strong movement verb.

**Principle:** into = movement ending in contact/inside; in = a static position.

**Memory tip:** into crosses a boundary; in is already inside.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Movement and Direction

questions.stem: The gymnast leapt \_\_\_ the beam and balanced \_\_\_ one foot.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** leapt onto the beam = movement onto a surface; balanced on one foot = position.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'leapt on the beam' can read as 'pounced on it'; 'balanced onto one foot' is wrong (onto = motion). (c) 'balanced onto one foot' is wrong. (d) 'leapt on the beam' loses the 'jump up and land on top' sense.

**Principle:** onto = movement onto a surface; on = position on a surface.

**Memory tip:** onto lands you on top; on keeps you there.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Movement and Direction

questions.stem: Explain the difference: (i) 'She walked into the room.' (ii) 'She was walking in the room.'
questions.answer: (i) into = she entered the room from outside (movement across the doorway). (ii) in = she was already inside, walking about within it. So (i) is about entering; (ii) is about moving around inside.
questions.solution:
**Answer:** (i) into = she entered the room from outside (movement across the doorway). (ii) in = she was already inside, walking about within it. So (i) is about entering; (ii) is about moving around inside.

**Why the other options are wrong:** Error: treating in and into as the same after a movement verb.

**Principle:** into = crossing into a space; in = movement or position within a space.

**Memory tip:** into = through the door; in = pacing around inside.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Movement and Direction

fields.Cognitive skill: Motion across a boundary vs motion within

questions.stem: The path runs \_\_\_ a thick forest and then \_\_\_ an open meadow to the river.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** through a forest = movement within an enclosing mass; across an open meadow = movement over a flat, open surface.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) swapped: 'across a forest' loses the 'among the trees' sense, and 'through an open meadow' wrongly treats open flat ground as enclosing. (c)/(d) apply one word to both.

**Principle:** through = within something enclosing (forest, tunnel, crowd, water); across = over a flat surface / side to side.

**Memory tip:** through = surrounded on all sides; across = over the top, edge to edge.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Movement and Direction

questions.stem: We strolled \_\_\_ the beach for an hour, then waded \_\_\_ the shallow stream to the other bank.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** along the beach = following its length; across the stream = from one side to the other.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'across the beach' = from sea to dunes (not the long walk intended); 'along the stream' = following its length (not crossing). (c)/(d) apply one word to both.

**Principle:** along = following the length of something; across = from one side to the other.

**Memory tip:** along = lengthwise; across = side to side.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Movement and Direction

questions.stem: The children ran \_\_\_ the tree, chasing each other in circles, before scrambling \_\_\_ the low wall.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** around the tree = in a circle / on all sides; over the low wall = across the top of a barrier.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'across the tree' is odd, and 'around the wall' = round its ends (not scrambling over it). (c) 'across the wall' loses the 'climb over' sense. (d) 'over the tree' is wrong (they circle it).

**Principle:** around = in a circle / on all sides; over = across the top of a barrier.

**Memory tip:** around = circling; over = climbing across the top.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Movement and Direction

questions.stem: She walked \_\_\_ the gate, opened it and went in; he only walked \_\_\_ the gate but turned back before reaching it.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** walked to the gate = reached it (a destination); walked towards the gate = moved in its direction without reaching it.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) swapped: reaching and using the gate needs 'to', and 'to the gate but turned back before reaching it' contradicts 'to' (which implies arrival). (c)/(d) apply one word to both and clash with 'reaching / not reaching'.

**Principle:** to = movement that reaches a destination; towards = movement in a direction, arrival not stated.

**Memory tip:** to = you get there; towards = you just face that way.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Movement and Direction

questions.stem: Explain the difference: (i) 'He ran to the exit.' (ii) 'He ran towards the exit.'
questions.answer: (i) to = he reached the exit (it was his destination). (ii) towards = he ran in the direction of the exit, but whether he reached it is not stated - he may have stopped or been interrupted.
questions.solution:
**Answer:** (i) to = he reached the exit (it was his destination). (ii) towards = he ran in the direction of the exit, but whether he reached it is not stated - he may have stopped or been interrupted.

**Why the other options are wrong:** Error: treating to and towards as identical.

**Principle:** to states arrival at a destination; towards states only the direction.

**Memory tip:** 'to' guarantees arrival; 'towards' only points the way.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Movement and Direction

questions.stem: The firefighter rushed \_\_\_ the stairs to the top floor, carried the child, and hurried back \_\_\_ to safety.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** up the stairs = to a higher place (the top floor); back down = to a lower place.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'rushed down the stairs to the top floor' contradicts 'top floor'. (c) 'hurried back up to safety' contradicts returning to the ground. (d) 'over the stairs' is wrong.

**Principle:** up = to a higher place; down = to a lower place.

**Memory tip:** up climbs, down descends - match direction to destination.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Movement and Direction

questions.stem: To reach the lake you walk \_\_\_ a narrow tunnel and then \_\_\_ an old mill on your right.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** through a narrow tunnel = movement inside an enclosing passage; past an old mill = going by it, leaving it behind.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'past a narrow tunnel' loses the 'go inside it' sense, and 'through an old mill' means entering the mill (not intended). (c) 'through an old mill' means entering it. (d) 'across a narrow tunnel' is wrong (a tunnel is entered, not crossed).

**Principle:** through = movement inside an enclosing thing; past = movement by/beyond an object.

**Memory tip:** through = you go inside it; past = you go by it.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Movement and Direction

questions.stem: The passengers got \_\_\_ the train at the wrong station and had to get \_\_\_ the next one.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** get off the train = leave a bus/train/plane; get on the next one = board it.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) reversed: boarding the wrong train then leaving the next contradicts the story. (c) 'get off the next one' is wrong. (d) 'got out the train' is wrong - we say get off a train (get out of is for cars).

**Principle:** get on / get off a bus, train, plane, ship; get in / get out of a car or taxi.

**Memory tip:** On/off large public transport; in/out of a car.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Movement and Direction

questions.stem: The cat shot \_\_\_ the frightened dog and darted \_\_\_ the room.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** away from the dog = fleeing, increasing distance; out of the room = exiting an enclosed space.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'out of the frightened dog' is wrong (a dog is not a container), and 'darted away from the room' weakens the 'exit through the door' sense. (c) 'darted away from the room' loses the exit sense. (d) 'from the dog' sounds like the cat originated from the dog; 'away from' is the natural fleeing phrase.

**Principle:** away from = movement increasing distance from something; out of = movement exiting an enclosed space.

**Memory tip:** away from = putting distance between; out of = coming out of a space.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Movement and Direction

questions.stem: Correct the movement preposition: 'The children ran across the tunnel to reach the playground.'
questions.answer: 'across the tunnel' should be 'through the tunnel': 'The children ran through the tunnel to reach the playground.'
questions.solution:
**Answer:** 'across the tunnel' should be 'through the tunnel': 'The children ran through the tunnel to reach the playground.'

**Why the other options are wrong:** Treating an enclosing passage (tunnel) as a flat surface to cross is the error; tunnels, forests and crowds take through.

**Principle:** through = movement inside an enclosing space; across = over a flat surface.

**Memory tip:** You go through a tunnel (inside it), not across it.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Movement and Direction

questions.stem: The cat jumped \_\_\_ the table, knocked a cup \_\_\_ the floor, and then curled up \_\_\_ a warm spot by the window.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** jumped onto the table (movement onto a surface); knocked a cup onto the floor (movement onto a surface); curled up in a warm spot (position within a spot).

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'jumped into the table' is wrong (a table is a surface, not a container). (c) 'knocked a cup into the floor' is wrong. (d) 'jumped on the table' loses the landing-movement (on = position).

**Principle:** onto = movement onto a surface; into = movement into a container; on/in = the resulting position.

**Memory tip:** onto lands you on a surface; into puts you inside a container.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Movement and Direction

questions.stem: Explain the difference: (i) 'The cat jumped onto the chair.' (ii) 'The cat sat on the chair.'
questions.answer: (i) onto shows movement - the cat moved from elsewhere up onto the chair. (ii) on shows position - the cat is simply resting there, no movement implied.
questions.solution:
**Answer:** (i) onto shows movement - the cat moved from elsewhere up onto the chair. (ii) on shows position - the cat is simply resting there, no movement implied.

**Why the other options are wrong:** Error: using on after a movement verb where onto is needed.

**Principle:** onto = movement to a surface; on = static position on a surface.

**Memory tip:** onto = the jump; on = the sitting.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Movement and Direction

questions.stem: To reach the stage she pushed her way \_\_\_ the packed crowd and then walked \_\_\_ the empty dance floor.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** through the packed crowd = moving amid a mass that surrounds you; across the empty dance floor = over a flat open surface.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'across the packed crowd' loses the 'in the midst of' sense, and 'through the empty dance floor' wrongly treats open flat ground as enclosing. (c)/(d) apply one word to both.

**Principle:** through = within/among an enclosing mass (crowd, forest, water); across = over a flat surface.

**Memory tip:** A crowd surrounds you -\> through; a floor is flat under you -\> across.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Movement and Direction

questions.stem: Translate the sentence \_\_\_ French, and write your answer neatly \_\_\_ the box provided.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** translate into + a language (fixed); write in the box = inside the box (a space).

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'translate in French' is wrong, and 'write into the box' overstates motion. (c) 'translate to French' is non-standard (translate into). (d) 'write on the box' = on its outer surface, not inside it.

**Principle:** translate into + a language; write in a box/space (inside) vs on a surface (outside).

**Memory tip:** You translate a text into a language; you write inside a box.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Movement and Direction

questions.stem: The skater stepped \_\_\_ the ice from the bench, glided for a while, and then stepped \_\_\_ again to rest.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** stepped onto the ice from the bench = movement onto a surface; stepped off again = leaving the surface.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'stepped on the ice' tends to mean 'trod on it'; with 'from the bench' the entry movement is onto. (c) 'stepped from the ice' is odd. (d) reversed.

**Principle:** onto = movement onto a surface; off = movement leaving a surface.

**Memory tip:** onto = getting on; off = getting off.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Movement and Direction

questions.stem: One moment the dog was in the garden; the next, it was in the kitchen. Rewrite as ONE sentence showing the movement, using 'out of' and 'into'.
questions.answer: For example: 'The dog ran out of the garden and into the kitchen.'
questions.solution:
**Answer:** For example: 'The dog ran out of the garden and into the kitchen.'

**Why the other options are wrong:** Using 'in' for both shows position, not the movement between the two places.

**Principle:** out of = movement leaving a space; into = movement entering a space.

**Memory tip:** Leaving a space -\> out of; entering a space -\> into.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Movement and Direction

fields.Cognitive skill: Expressing movement with out of / into

questions.stem: One movement preposition is wrong. Identify and correct: 'He walked into the bridge to cross the river.'
questions.answer: 'walked into the bridge' should be 'walked onto the bridge' (or 'across the bridge'): 'He walked onto the bridge to cross the river.'
questions.solution:
**Answer:** 'walked into the bridge' should be 'walked onto the bridge' (or 'across the bridge'): 'He walked onto the bridge to cross the river.'

**Why the other options are wrong:** 'into the bridge' wrongly treats a bridge as something you enter; you step onto its surface / walk across it.

**Principle:** onto/across for a surface such as a bridge; into for entering an enclosed space.

**Memory tip:** A bridge is a surface -\> onto/across, not into.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Movement and Direction

fields.Cognitive skill: into vs onto with a bridge

questions.stem: Complete with movement prepositions. A: How do I get to the roof? B: Go \_\_\_ these stairs to the top, then step \_\_\_ the flat roof through the small door.
questions.solution:
**Answer:** up (these stairs) ... onto (the flat roof).

**Why the other options are wrong:** 'go on these stairs' is wrong (should be up); 'step into the flat roof' is wrong (a roof is a surface -\> onto, not into).

**Principle:** up = ascending; onto = movement onto a surface.

**Memory tip:** up the stairs, onto the roof (a surface).
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Movement and Direction

questions.stem: Choose the option that fits: 'The parade winds \_\_\_ the narrow lanes of the old town, passes \_\_\_ the town hall, and ends \_\_\_ the main square.'
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** through the narrow lanes = winding along enclosed lanes; past the town hall = going by it; in the main square = inside an open square.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'across the narrow lanes' loses the winding-along sense. (c) 'into the narrow lanes' = merely entering them. (d) 'passes into the town hall' = entering the building (wrong; the parade goes by it).

**Principle:** through = amid/along enclosed lanes; past = going by without entering; in + an open square.

**Memory tip:** through the lanes, past the hall (not into it), in the square.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Movement and Direction

options.label: A
options.text: Listen to me and I'll explain the plan to you.

options.label: B
options.text: Listen me and I'll explain you the plan.

options.label: C
options.text: Listen to me and I'll explain you the plan.

options.label: D
options.text: Listen me and I'll explain the plan to you.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** listen takes to before the person (listen to me); explain takes to before the person (explain something to someone), never 'explain someone'.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'listen me' drops to and 'explain you' drops to. (c) 'explain you the plan' - explain needs 'to' before the person. (d) 'listen me' - listen needs 'to'. These reflect dropping the preposition (a Hindi-influenced pattern).

**Principle:** listen to someone; explain something to someone.

**Memory tip:** You always listen TO; you explain something TO a person.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Verbs and Their Prepositions

options.label: B
options.text: The squad comprises of eleven players.

options.label: C
options.text: The squad is consisted of eleven players.

options.label: D
options.text: The squad consist of eleven players.

questions.stem: Which sentence about a squad is correct?
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** comprise takes NO 'of' - it already means 'be made up of'.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'comprises of' wrongly borrows the 'of' from 'consists of'/'composed of'. (c) 'is consisted of' - consist has no passive form. (d) 'consist' disagrees with the singular subject and 'consist of' is the correct verb - it should be 'consists of'.

**Principle:** comprise (no of); consist of; be composed of - never 'comprise of' or 'is consisted of'.

**Memory tip:** 'comprise' already contains 'of' in its meaning - don't add it.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Verbs and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: Explain the difference: (i) 'I don't believe you.' (ii) 'I don't believe in you.'
questions.answer: (i) believe you = I don't accept that what you are saying is true (I think you are mistaken or lying about this). (ii) believe in you = I don't have faith or confidence in you or your abilities. So (i) is about one statement; (ii) is about trust in the person overall.
questions.solution:
**Answer:** (i) believe you = I don't accept that what you are saying is true (I think you are mistaken or lying about this). (ii) believe in you = I don't have faith or confidence in you or your abilities. So (i) is about one statement; (ii) is about trust in the person overall.

**Why the other options are wrong:** Error: assuming the 'in' is optional or decorative. It changes the meaning completely.

**Principle:** believe someone = accept their statement; believe in someone = trust / have faith in them.

**Memory tip:** believe you = 'I trust this statement'; believe in you = 'I trust who you are'.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Verbs and Their Prepositions

fields.Cognitive skill: Meaning shift with a dependent preposition

questions.stem: I agree \_\_\_ you that the plan is risky, but in the end, although I still disliked it, I had to agree \_\_\_ their decision.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** agree with a person/opinion = share it; agree to a proposal/plan = consent to it. Because he 'still disliked it', he could only consent (agree to), not share the opinion.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'agree to you' is wrong, and 'agree with their decision' contradicts 'still disliked it'. (c) 'agree with their decision' contradicts disliking it (you can't share an opinion you dislike). (d) 'agree on you' is wrong (agree on = settle a matter jointly).

**Principle:** agree with a person/opinion (share it); agree to a proposal (consent); agree on a matter (settle it together).

**Memory tip:** with = same opinion; to = say yes to a plan; on = settle a matter together.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Verbs and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: Whom does this bag belong \_\_\_? It certainly doesn't belong \_\_\_ me.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** belong to someone = be owned by that person.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'belong with' means 'go together with' (not ownership). (c) 'belong with me' would mean 'go together with me', not 'be owned by me'. (d) dropping 'to' after belong is wrong.

**Principle:** belong to someone = be owned by; belong with = go together with.

**Memory tip:** Ownership -\> belong to.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Verbs and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: Choose the option: 'The babysitter has to \_\_\_ the children while their mother \_\_\_ a new job online.'
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** look after = take care of (the children); look for = search for (a job).

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) swapped: 'look for the children' = search for them; 'looks after a new job' = takes care of a job. (c) 'look at the children' = merely watch them. (d) 'looks at a new job' = examines one job, not searching.

**Principle:** look after = take care of; look for = search for; look at = direct your eyes at.

**Memory tip:** after = care for; for = search; at = point your eyes.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Verbs and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: Correct any error: 'He requested for a glass of water and asked for the time.'
questions.answer: 'requested for a glass of water' should be 'requested a glass of water' (request is transitive - no 'for'). 'asked for the time' is correct. Corrected: 'He requested a glass of water and asked for the time.'
questions.solution:
**Answer:** 'requested for a glass of water' should be 'requested a glass of water' (request is transitive - no 'for'). 'asked for the time' is correct. Corrected: 'He requested a glass of water and asked for the time.'

**Why the other options are wrong:** Adding 'for' after request is a common Indian-English error; request takes a direct object, unlike 'ask for'.

**Principle:** request + object (no for); ask for + object.

**Memory tip:** You request something, but you ask for something.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Verbs and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: She apologised \_\_\_ her teacher \_\_\_ arriving late.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** apologise to + the person, for + the offence.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'apologise with' is wrong. (c) 'apologise of' is wrong. (d) reversed order and prepositions.

**Principle:** apologise to + person, for + the thing done.

**Memory tip:** You say sorry TO a person FOR a deed.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Verbs and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: Heavy rain prevented the match \_\_\_ taking place.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** prevent someone/something from + gerund.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'prevented to take place' is a calque (prevent to do). (c) 'prevent of' is wrong. (d) 'prevent for' is wrong.

**Principle:** prevent / stop / keep someone from doing something (+ -ing).

**Memory tip:** prevent FROM doing - it blocks the action.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Verbs and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: The customers complained \_\_\_ the manager \_\_\_ the poor service.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** complain to + the person you tell; complain about + the problem.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) reverses the roles and makes nonsense. (c) 'complain with' is wrong. (d) 'complain of' is for a symptom/ailment ('complain of a headache'), not a service you report.

**Principle:** complain to + person; complain about + thing; complain of + a symptom.

**Memory tip:** You complain TO a person ABOUT a problem.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Verbs and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: We arrived \_\_\_ the airport at noon and finally arrived \_\_\_ Delhi by evening.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** arrive at + a place/building (airport); arrive in + a city (Delhi).

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) swapped. (c) 'arrive at Delhi' - a city takes in. (d) 'arrive to' is a calque; arrive never takes 'to'.

**Principle:** arrive at + a point/building/small place; arrive in + a town/country; never 'arrive to'.

**Memory tip:** at a spot, in a big place; never 'arrive to'.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Verbs and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: Rescuers searched \_\_\_ the missing hikers all night.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** search for = try to find (someone/something). (Note: 'search a place' - transitive - means look through it: 'searched the cave for treasure'.)

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'searched the missing hikers' would mean searching the hikers' bodies. (c) 'search about' is wrong. (d) 'search to' is wrong.

**Principle:** search for + what you want to find; search + a place you look through.

**Memory tip:** search FOR the thing you want; search a place you rummage through.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Verbs and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: My grandmother suffers \_\_\_ arthritis.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** suffer from + a named illness/condition.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'suffer of' is a calque. (c) 'suffer with' is colloquial for enduring an ache, but the standard with a named condition is 'suffer from'. (d) 'suffer arthritis' - suffer is transitive only for events ('suffer a defeat'), not illnesses.

**Principle:** suffer from + an illness/condition.

**Memory tip:** For an illness, you suffer FROM it.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Verbs and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: It's unkind to laugh \_\_\_ someone who makes a mistake.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** laugh at someone = mock/ridicule them.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'laugh on' is a calque. (c) 'laugh of' is wrong. (d) 'laugh with' means share friendly laughter, not mock a mistake.

**Principle:** laugh at = mock; laugh with = share amusement.

**Memory tip:** Mocking -\> laugh AT; sharing -\> laugh WITH.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Verbs and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: All students are encouraged to participate \_\_\_ the science fair.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** participate in + an activity/event.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'participate at' is wrong. (c) 'participate on' is wrong. (d) 'participate to' is a French calque ('participer a').

**Principle:** participate in + an activity/event.

**Memory tip:** You take part IN something.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Verbs and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: He insisted \_\_\_ paying for everyone's tickets.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** insist on + noun/gerund.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'insisted to pay' is a calque. (c) 'insist in' is wrong. (d) 'insist for' is wrong.

**Principle:** insist on + noun/gerund.

**Memory tip:** insist ON doing.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Verbs and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: Do you object \_\_\_ my opening the window?
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** object to + noun/gerund. Because 'to' here is a preposition, a gerund follows ('opening'), not an infinitive.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'object against' is redundant (object already means 'be against'). (c) 'object on' is wrong. (d) 'object for' is wrong.

**Principle:** object to + noun/gerund (the 'to' is a preposition -\> -ing).

**Memory tip:** object TO something; and 'object to opening', not 'object to open'.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Verbs and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: I'm really looking forward \_\_\_ you again soon.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** In 'look forward to', 'to' is a preposition, so it is followed by the -ing form (seeing).

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'look forward to see' is the classic error - treating 'to' as an infinitive marker. (c) 'look forward for' is wrong. (d) 'look forward at' is wrong.

**Principle:** In 'look forward to', 'to' is a preposition -\> followed by -ing, not the base verb.

**Memory tip:** You can 'look forward to it' - so 'to' is a preposition -\> 'look forward to seeing'.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Verbs and Their Prepositions

options.label: A
options.text: 'She is used to waking up early.'

options.label: B
options.text: 'She is used to wake up early.'

questions.stem: Which of these are correct? Select ALL that apply.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** 'be used to', 'confess to' and 'resort to' all have 'to' as a preposition, so a gerund follows: 'used to waking', 'confessed to taking', 'resorted to cheating'.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'is used to wake up early' is wrong: 'be used to' (accustomed) needs -ing. The base-verb pattern belongs to a different structure, 'used to + base verb' (a past habit), which does not fit 'She is used to \_\_\_'.

**Principle:** 'be/get used to', 'confess to', 'resort to', 'object to', 'look forward to' all take -ing.

**Memory tip:** If you can replace the noun after 'to' with 'it', 'to' is a preposition -\> use -ing.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Verbs and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: Correct any error: 'Let's discuss about the project during lunch.'
questions.answer: 'discuss about the project' should be 'discuss the project' (discuss is transitive - no 'about'). Corrected: 'Let's discuss the project during lunch.'
questions.solution:
**Answer:** 'discuss about the project' should be 'discuss the project' (discuss is transitive - no 'about'). Corrected: 'Let's discuss the project during lunch.'

**Why the other options are wrong:** Adding 'about' after discuss is a common Indian-English error; discuss, mention and describe take a direct object.

**Principle:** discuss + object (no about).

**Memory tip:** You discuss something, not 'discuss about' it. (Compare: 'talk about'.)
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Verbs and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: Correct any error: 'The students entered into the hall quietly.'
questions.answer: 'entered into the hall' should be 'entered the hall' (enter a place is transitive; 'enter into' is only for abstract things such as agreements). Corrected: 'The students entered the hall quietly.'
questions.solution:
**Answer:** 'entered into the hall' should be 'entered the hall' (enter a place is transitive; 'enter into' is only for abstract things such as agreements). Corrected: 'The students entered the hall quietly.'

**Why the other options are wrong:** Adding 'into' after enter for a physical place is the error; 'enter into' is reserved for agreements, contracts and discussions.

**Principle:** enter + a place (no into); enter into + an agreement/discussion.

**Memory tip:** You enter a room, but you enter into a deal.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Verbs and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: Correct any error: 'Please return back the library book by Friday.'
questions.answer: 'return back' should be 'return' (return already means 'give/go back', so 'back' is redundant). Corrected: 'Please return the library book by Friday.'
questions.solution:
**Answer:** 'return back' should be 'return' (return already means 'give/go back', so 'back' is redundant). Corrected: 'Please return the library book by Friday.'

**Why the other options are wrong:** Adding 'back' after return is redundant (like 'repeat again', 'revert back').

**Principle:** return = give/go back; do not add 'back'.

**Memory tip:** 'return' already contains 'back' - don't say it twice.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Verbs and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: The referee accused the striker \_\_\_ diving and blamed him \_\_\_ the delay.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** accuse someone of (doing) something; blame someone for something.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) swapped: 'accuse for' and 'blame of' are both wrong. (c) 'blame of' is wrong. (d) 'accuse with' is wrong.

**Principle:** accuse of; blame for (but note 'blame something on someone').

**Memory tip:** accuse OF a wrong; blame FOR a result.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Verbs and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: Let me congratulate you \_\_\_ your success - it reminds me \_\_\_ my own first prize.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** congratulate someone on something; remind someone of something = make them recall it.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'congratulate for' is a common error (standard is 'on'), and 'remind about' is for prompting about a task, not triggering a memory. (c) 'remind about my first prize' would mean 'prompt me to deal with it'; here the sense is 'brings the memory back' -\> of. (d) 'congratulate for' is the error.

**Principle:** congratulate on; remind of (trigger a memory) vs remind about (prompt about a task).

**Memory tip:** congratulate ON an achievement; something reminds you OF a memory.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Verbs and Their Prepositions

fields.Cognitive skill: congratulate on / remind of vs about

questions.stem: One preposition is wrong. Identify and correct: 'She married with a doctor she met at college.'
questions.answer: 'married with a doctor' should be 'married a doctor' (marry is transitive - no 'with'). You may also say 'She got married to a doctor.' Corrected: 'She married a doctor she met at college.'
questions.solution:
**Answer:** 'married with a doctor' should be 'married a doctor' (marry is transitive - no 'with'). You may also say 'She got married to a doctor.' Corrected: 'She married a doctor she met at college.'

**Why the other options are wrong:** 'marry with' is a calque (from Hindi/Spanish); marry takes a direct object, or use 'be/get married to someone'.

**Principle:** marry someone (no with); be married TO someone.

**Memory tip:** You marry someone, or are married TO them - never 'married with'.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Verbs and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: Complete with the right prepositions. A: What happened in the meeting? B: They asked me to explain the delay \_\_\_ the whole team, and then congratulated me \_\_\_ finishing the report early.
questions.answer: to (the whole team) ... on (finishing the report).
questions.solution:
**Answer:** to (the whole team) ... on (finishing the report).

**Why the other options are wrong:** 'explain the whole team' is wrong (needs 'to'); 'congratulated me for' is non-standard (use 'on').

**Principle:** explain something to someone; congratulate someone on something.

**Memory tip:** explain TO people; congratulate ON an achievement.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Verbs and Their Prepositions

fields.Cognitive skill: explain to / congratulate on in context

questions.stem: She's very good \_\_\_ mathematics but rather bad \_\_\_ spelling.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** good at / bad at + a skill, subject or activity.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'good in mathematics' is a calque; standard English uses 'good at' for a skill. (c) 'bad in spelling' is wrong. (d) 'good with' is for handling things or people ('good with children'), not a subject.

**Principle:** good/bad at + a skill/subject/activity; good with + tools/people you handle.

**Memory tip:** You're good AT a skill; good WITH people or things.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Adjectives and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: He has always been interested \_\_\_ astronomy and fascinated \_\_\_ black holes.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** interested in + a topic; fascinated by (or with) something.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'fascinated in' is wrong. (c) 'interested about' is wrong. (d) 'interested on' is wrong.

**Principle:** interested in; fascinated by/with.

**Memory tip:** interested IN a topic; fascinated BY something amazing.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Adjectives and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: The toddler is afraid \_\_\_ the dark and scared \_\_\_ loud noises.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** afraid of / scared of / frightened of.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b)/(c) 'afraid/scared from' is a calque (from Hindi 'se darna'). (d) 'afraid with' is wrong.

**Principle:** afraid of / scared of / frightened of.

**Memory tip:** Fear takes OF, not 'from'.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Adjectives and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: The captain was proud \_\_\_ her team and felt responsible \_\_\_ their training.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** proud of + someone/something; responsible for + a duty/result.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) swapped. (c) 'responsible of' is wrong. (d) 'proud about' is colloquial; standard is 'proud of'.

**Principle:** proud of + someone/something; responsible for + a duty/result.

**Memory tip:** proud OF; responsible FOR.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Adjectives and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: Her handwriting is quite different \_\_\_ mine, though in some ways it is similar \_\_\_ my sister's.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** different from; similar to.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'different than' is accepted in some US speech, but formal/SAT English prefers 'different from'. (c) 'different to' is BrE colloquial, and 'similar from' is wrong. (d) 'similar from' is wrong.

**Principle:** different from; similar to; identical to.

**Memory tip:** different FROM; similar/identical TO.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Adjectives and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: The coach was angry \_\_\_ the players and angry \_\_\_ their careless mistakes.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** angry with + a person; angry about + a thing or situation. ('Angry at a person' is common in American English, but the mistake still takes 'about', not 'with'.)

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'angry with their mistakes' is wrong (a thing takes about/at, not with). (c) 'angry about the players' treats people as a situation. (d) 'angry with their mistakes' - mistakes take about, not with.

**Principle:** angry with + a person; angry about + a thing/situation.

**Memory tip:** angry WITH a person; angry ABOUT a thing.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Adjectives and Their Prepositions

fields.Cognitive skill: angry with vs about (person vs thing)

questions.stem: The town is famous \_\_\_ its silk and known \_\_\_ its ancient temple.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** famous for / known for + the quality or product it is celebrated for.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'famous as' = famous in the role of ('famous as a singer'), not for a product. (c) 'known as' = called/named, a different meaning. (d) 'famous by' is wrong.

**Principle:** famous/known for + a quality or product; famous/known as + a role or name.

**Memory tip:** for a quality; as a role/name.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Adjectives and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: Explain the difference: (i) 'She is famous as a poet.' (ii) 'She is famous for her poems.'
questions.answer: (i) as = in her role/capacity - she is well known in the role of a poet. (ii) for = because of the thing that made her famous - her poems. So (i) names what she is; (ii) names what she is celebrated for.
questions.solution:
**Answer:** (i) as = in her role/capacity - she is well known in the role of a poet. (ii) for = because of the thing that made her famous - her poems. So (i) names what she is; (ii) names what she is celebrated for.

**Why the other options are wrong:** Error: swapping as (role) and for (reason).

**Principle:** famous as + a role; famous for + the reason/quality.

**Memory tip:** as = the hat she wears; for = the reason people know her.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Adjectives and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: By the end she was tired \_\_\_ his constant excuses.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** tired of = bored / fed up with. (Note: 'tired from' means physically exhausted by an effort - 'tired from running'.)

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'tired from' means worn out by an activity; here the sense is 'fed up', so 'of'. (c) 'tired with' is non-standard here. (d) 'tired by' is wrong.

**Principle:** tired of = fed up with; tired from = exhausted by an effort.

**Memory tip:** Fed up -\> tired OF; worn out -\> tired FROM.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Adjectives and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: In 'We were all surprised \_\_\_ the news', are both 'at' and 'by' acceptable? Explain any nuance.
questions.answer: Yes - both are correct. 'surprised by' slightly emphasises the news as the cause/agent that produced the surprise; 'surprised at' slightly emphasises your reaction to it. In everyday use they are interchangeable here.
questions.solution:
**Answer:** Yes - both are correct. 'surprised by' slightly emphasises the news as the cause/agent that produced the surprise; 'surprised at' slightly emphasises your reaction to it. In everyday use they are interchangeable here.

**Why the other options are wrong:** Errors: thinking only one is allowed; or using 'surprised of'/'surprised from' (both wrong).

**Principle:** surprised at / surprised by are both standard; 'surprised of/from' are not.

**Memory tip:** by = what caused it; at = your reaction - both fine; never 'of/from'.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Adjectives and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: The teacher was pleased \_\_\_ our project but a little worried \_\_\_ the deadline.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** pleased with + something you produced; worried about + a concern.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) swapped. (c) 'worried with' is wrong. (d) 'pleased at' occurs with an event ('pleased at the result'), but with a thing you made 'pleased with' is standard; the second blank still needs 'about'.

**Principle:** pleased with + someone/something; worried about + a concern.

**Memory tip:** pleased WITH; worried ABOUT.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Adjectives and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: She is capable \_\_\_ great things, perfectly suitable \_\_\_ the role, and ready \_\_\_ any challenge.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** capable of; suitable for; ready for + a noun.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'capable for' and 'suitable of' are wrong. (c) 'suitable to' is less standard than 'suitable for'. (d) 'ready to' takes a verb ('ready to face'), not a noun; before a noun it is 'ready for'.

**Principle:** capable of; suitable for; ready for + noun (but ready to + verb).

**Memory tip:** capable OF; suitable/ready FOR a thing.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Adjectives and Their Prepositions

fields.Cognitive skill: capable of / suitable for / ready for

questions.stem: Are you aware \_\_\_ the risks? Despite them, he's very fond \_\_\_ rock climbing.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** aware of; fond of.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'aware about' is wrong. (c) 'fond for' is wrong. (d) 'aware with' is wrong.

**Principle:** aware of; fond of.

**Memory tip:** aware OF; fond OF.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Adjectives and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: Correct the adjective + preposition errors: 'He is very keen in football and good in defending.'
questions.answer: 'keen in football' should be 'keen on football'; 'good in defending' should be 'good at defending'. Corrected: 'He is very keen on football and good at defending.'
questions.solution:
**Answer:** 'keen in football' should be 'keen on football'; 'good in defending' should be 'good at defending'. Corrected: 'He is very keen on football and good at defending.'

**Why the other options are wrong:** Errors: 'keen in' (should be keen on + noun) and 'good in' an activity (should be good at).

**Principle:** keen on + noun; good at + activity/skill.

**Memory tip:** keen ON; good AT an activity.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Adjectives and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: As a teenager he was still dependent \_\_\_ his parents, but he longed to be independent \_\_\_ them.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** dependent on; independent of.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) swapped. (c) 'independent from' is a calque; standard is 'independent of'. (d) 'independent to' is wrong.

**Principle:** dependent on; independent of.

**Memory tip:** dependent ON (leaning on); independent OF (free of).
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Adjectives and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: Many people think this phone is superior \_\_\_ the older model, and they prefer it \_\_\_ any other brand.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** superior to; prefer X to Y. Both take 'to', never 'than'.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b)/(c) 'superior than' and 'prefer than' are errors by false analogy with comparatives like 'better than'. (d) 'superior from' is wrong.

**Principle:** superior/inferior/senior/junior/prior to; prefer X to Y - all take 'to', not 'than'.

**Memory tip:** These Latin-based words take TO, not 'than'.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Adjectives and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: The table is made \_\_\_ solid oak, paper is made \_\_\_ wood pulp, and this cake is made \_\_\_ real butter.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** made of solid oak (material still recognisable); made from wood pulp (material transformed into something new); made with real butter (one ingredient among others).

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b)/(c)/(d) swap the three: 'made from oak' misses that the oak is still visibly oak; 'made of wood pulp' misses the transformation into paper; 'made of butter' would mean the cake is entirely butter.

**Principle:** made of = material still recognisable; made from = material transformed; made with = one ingredient used.

**Memory tip:** of = you can still see it; from = it became something new; with = one ingredient in the mix.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Adjectives and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: Explain the difference: (i) 'Wine is made from grapes.' (ii) 'The bowl is made of glass.'
questions.answer: (i) made from = the original material (grapes) has been transformed and is no longer recognisable in the product. (ii) made of = the material (glass) is still present and recognisable in the finished object. So 'from' signals a transformation; 'of' signals the material is unchanged.
questions.solution:
