**Answer:** (i) made from = the original material (grapes) has been transformed and is no longer recognisable in the product. (ii) made of = the material (glass) is still present and recognisable in the finished object. So 'from' signals a transformation; 'of' signals the material is unchanged.

**Why the other options are wrong:** Error: using 'of' when the material has changed form, or 'from' when it has not.

**Principle:** made of = unchanged material; made from = transformed material.

**Memory tip:** If you can still 'see' the material, use of; if it turned into something new, use from.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Adjectives and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: Which are standard/correct? Select ALL that apply.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** married to, allergic to and jealous of are the standard combinations.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (c) 'guilty for' is wrong - it should be 'guilty of the crime'. (Note the near neighbour 'responsible for' does take 'for', which makes 'guilty for' tempting.)

**Principle:** married to; allergic to; jealous of; guilty of.

**Memory tip:** guilty OF a crime, not 'for'.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Adjectives and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: I'm grateful \_\_\_ you \_\_\_ your help.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** grateful to + the person, for + the thing.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) swapped. (c) 'grateful with' is wrong. (d) 'grateful of' is wrong.

**Principle:** grateful/thankful to + person, for + the thing.

**Memory tip:** grateful TO a person FOR a favour.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Adjectives and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: One or more prepositions are wrong. Identify and correct: 'The results were consistent to our earlier findings and similar with last year's.'
questions.answer: 'consistent to' should be 'consistent with'; 'similar with' should be 'similar to'. Corrected: 'The results were consistent with our earlier findings and similar to last year's.'
questions.solution:
**Answer:** 'consistent to' should be 'consistent with'; 'similar with' should be 'similar to'. Corrected: 'The results were consistent with our earlier findings and similar to last year's.'

**Why the other options are wrong:** consistent takes 'with' (not 'to'); similar takes 'to' (not 'with'). They are easy to swap.

**Principle:** consistent with; similar to.

**Memory tip:** consistent WITH; similar TO - don't cross them.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Adjectives and Their Prepositions

questions.stem: Choose the best option: 'She was anxious \_\_\_ the interview because she felt she was bad \_\_\_ answering tricky questions, though she was keen \_\_\_ getting the job.'
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** anxious about (worried); bad at + an activity; keen on + a noun.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'anxious for' means eagerly wanting ('anxious for news'), and 'bad in' is wrong. (c) 'bad in' is wrong. (d) 'anxious of' is wrong.

**Principle:** anxious about (worried) vs anxious for (eager); bad at + activity; keen on + noun.

**Memory tip:** worried -\> anxious ABOUT; skill -\> bad AT; enthusiasm -\> keen ON.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Adjectives and Their Prepositions

fields.Cognitive skill: anxious about/for, bad at, keen on

questions.stem: State whether the preposition is unnecessary, missing, wrong, or correct - then fix if needed: 'The principal emphasised on the need for discipline.'
questions.answer: Unnecessary preposition. 'emphasised on' should be 'emphasised' (emphasise is transitive - it takes a direct object). Corrected: 'The principal emphasised the need for discipline.'
questions.solution:
**Answer:** Unnecessary preposition. 'emphasised on' should be 'emphasised' (emphasise is transitive - it takes a direct object). Corrected: 'The principal emphasised the need for discipline.'

**Why the other options are wrong:** The noun phrase 'put emphasis ON' misleads people into adding 'on' to the verb; the verb 'emphasise' takes no preposition.

**Principle:** emphasise + object (no on); but 'lay/put emphasis on'.

**Memory tip:** The verb emphasises something directly - drop the 'on'.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Unnecessary, Wrong, Missing or Correct

questions.stem: State whether the preposition is unnecessary, missing, wrong, or correct - then fix if needed: 'Please reply to my email by tomorrow.'
questions.answer: Correct - no change needed. 'reply to' is right: reply is intransitive and needs 'to' before the thing replied to.
questions.solution:
**Answer:** Correct - no change needed. 'reply to' is right: reply is intransitive and needs 'to' before the thing replied to.

**Why the other options are wrong:** The trap is 'correcting' a sentence that is already right (or dropping 'to' to make 'reply my email', which is wrong).

**Principle:** reply to + something/someone (but 'answer' takes no 'to': answer the email).

**Memory tip:** You reply TO a message, but you answer it (no 'to').
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Unnecessary, Wrong, Missing or Correct

questions.stem: State whether the preposition is unnecessary, missing, wrong, or correct - then fix if needed: 'He could not cope up with the pressure.'
questions.answer: Unnecessary word. 'cope up with' should be 'cope with' ('up' is redundant). Corrected: 'He could not cope with the pressure.'
questions.solution:
**Answer:** Unnecessary word. 'cope up with' should be 'cope with' ('up' is redundant). Corrected: 'He could not cope with the pressure.'

**Why the other options are wrong:** 'cope up with' is a common calque; the correct phrasal verb is just 'cope with'.

**Principle:** cope with + a difficulty (no 'up').

**Memory tip:** You cope WITH something - there is no 'up' in it.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Unnecessary, Wrong, Missing or Correct

questions.stem: State whether the preposition is unnecessary, missing, wrong, or correct - then fix if needed: 'The child resembles to his father.'
questions.answer: Unnecessary preposition. 'resembles to' should be 'resembles' (resemble is transitive). Corrected: 'The child resembles his father.'
questions.solution:
**Answer:** Unnecessary preposition. 'resembles to' should be 'resembles' (resemble is transitive). Corrected: 'The child resembles his father.'

**Why the other options are wrong:** By analogy with 'similar to', people wrongly add 'to'; resemble takes a direct object.

**Principle:** resemble + object (no to); compare 'bears a resemblance to'.

**Memory tip:** You resemble someone directly - drop the 'to'.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Unnecessary, Wrong, Missing or Correct

questions.stem: State whether the preposition is unnecessary, missing, wrong, or correct - then fix if needed: 'We reached to the station just in time.'
questions.answer: Unnecessary preposition. 'reached to the station' should be 'reached the station' (reach a place is transitive). Corrected: 'We reached the station just in time.'
questions.solution:
**Answer:** Unnecessary preposition. 'reached to the station' should be 'reached the station' (reach a place is transitive). Corrected: 'We reached the station just in time.'

**Why the other options are wrong:** People add 'to' by analogy with 'got to/arrived at'; reach takes the place as a direct object.

**Principle:** reach + a place/level (no to): 'reach the top', 'reach the station'.

**Memory tip:** You reach a place directly - no 'to'.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Unnecessary, Wrong, Missing or Correct

options.label: A
options.text: She explained the rules to the new players.

options.label: B
options.text: She explained the new players the rules.

options.label: C
options.text: She explained about the rules to the new players.

options.label: D
options.text: She explained the rules with the new players.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** explain + something + to + someone. You cannot 'explain someone something', and no 'about' is needed.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'explain someone something' uses a double object, which explain does not allow. (c) 'explain about' adds an unnecessary 'about'. (d) 'explain ... with' is wrong - it should be 'to'.

**Principle:** explain something to someone (no double object, no 'about').

**Memory tip:** explain the thing TO the person.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Unnecessary, Wrong, Missing or Correct

questions.stem: State whether the particle is needed, unnecessary, or wrong - then explain: 'The manager will look into the matter.'
questions.answer: Needed and correct. 'look into' is a phrasal verb meaning 'investigate'; the 'into' is essential and cannot be dropped.
questions.solution:
**Answer:** Needed and correct. 'look into' is a phrasal verb meaning 'investigate'; the 'into' is essential and cannot be dropped.

**Why the other options are wrong:** The trap is deleting 'into' as if it were redundant; 'look the matter' is meaningless, and 'look at the matter' changes the sense to 'view' rather than 'investigate'.

**Principle:** look into = investigate (the particle carries the meaning).

**Memory tip:** look INTO = dig into / investigate.

questions.stem: State whether there is a preposition error, and fix it if so: 'They discussed the plan and then voted for it.'
questions.answer: Correct - no change needed. 'discuss' correctly takes a direct object (no 'about'), and 'vote for' is the right combination.
questions.solution:
**Answer:** Correct - no change needed. 'discuss' correctly takes a direct object (no 'about'), and 'vote for' is the right combination.

**Why the other options are wrong:** The trap is adding 'about' after discuss, or changing 'vote for'. Both are already correct here.

**Principle:** discuss + object (no about); vote for + something.

**Memory tip:** discuss it directly; vote FOR it.

questions.stem: State whether the preposition is unnecessary, missing, wrong, or correct - then fix if needed: 'She is not interested to join the club.'

questions.solution:
**Answer:** Wrong preposition/structure. 'interested to join' should be 'interested in joining' (interested in + gerund). Corrected: 'She is not interested in joining the club.'

**Why the other options are wrong:** 'interested to + verb' is used only with a few verbs of reaction ('interested to hear/know'); to talk about an activity you want to do, use 'interested in + -ing'.

**Principle:** interested in + noun/gerund.

**Memory tip:** interested IN doing something.

questions.stem: State whether the preposition is unnecessary, missing, wrong, or correct - then fix if needed: 'Please listen the instructions carefully.'

**Why the other options are wrong:** Dropping 'to' after listen is a common error; listen is intransitive and needs 'to' before its object.

**Principle:** listen to + something/someone.

**Memory tip:** You listen TO something.

questions.stem: State whether the preposition is unnecessary, missing, wrong, or correct - then fix if needed: 'The results depend the weather.'

**Answer:** Missing preposition. It should be 'depend on the weather'. Corrected: 'The results depend on the weather.'

**Why the other options are wrong:** Dropping 'on' leaves depend without its required preposition.

**Principle:** depend on + something.

**Memory tip:** You depend ON something.

questions.stem: State whether the preposition is unnecessary, missing, wrong, or correct - then fix if needed: 'Divide this cake in four pieces.'

**Principle:** divide/split/cut something into + parts.

**Memory tip:** Breaking into parts -\> into, not in.

questions.answer: Correct - no change needed. 'congratulations on + something' is the standard combination.

**Answer:** Correct - no change needed. 'congratulations on + something' is the standard combination.

**Why the other options are wrong:** The trap is changing 'on' to 'for'; congratulations/congratulate take 'on'.

**Principle:** congratulations on / congratulate someone on + an achievement.

**Memory tip:** congratulate ON an achievement.

questions.stem: Is 'on' unnecessary, wrong, or acceptable-with-a-different-meaning here? 'She threw the ball on the roof.'
questions.answer: Acceptable, but it changes the meaning. 'on the roof' is grammatical and means the ball ended up resting on the roof. If you mean the action of landing it up there, 'onto the roof' is clearer; if it went right over, 'over the roof'. So 'on' is not an error - it just fixes the ball on the roof rather than stressing the movement.
questions.solution:
**Answer:** Acceptable, but it changes the meaning. 'on the roof' is grammatical and means the ball ended up resting on the roof. If you mean the action of landing it up there, 'onto the roof' is clearer; if it went right over, 'over the roof'. So 'on' is not an error - it just fixes the ball on the roof rather than stressing the movement.

**Why the other options are wrong:** The trap is calling it simply 'right' or 'wrong'; the honest answer is that the preposition is acceptable but shifts the meaning (resting-position vs movement).

**Principle:** on = resting position; onto = movement onto a surface; over = across the top.

**Memory tip:** on = it sits there; onto = it lands there; over = it clears it.

questions.stem: Only one sentence is correct. Which one?
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** apply takes 'for' (apply for leave/a job). request, demand and order are transitive verbs and take no 'for'.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (a) 'requested for' -\> request (no for). (c) 'demanded for' -\> demand (no for). (d) 'ordered for' -\> order (no for).

**Principle:** apply for + something; but request/demand/order + object (no 'for').

**Memory tip:** You apply FOR leave, but you request/demand it directly.

questions.stem: State whether the preposition/structure is correct, and fix it if not: 'The teacher asked a question to the class.'
questions.answer: Non-standard structure. Standard English is 'asked the class a question' (ask + someone + something), or 'put a question to the class'. Corrected: 'The teacher asked the class a question.'
questions.solution:
**Answer:** Non-standard structure. Standard English is 'asked the class a question' (ask + someone + something), or 'put a question to the class'. Corrected: 'The teacher asked the class a question.'

**Why the other options are wrong:** 'ask a question to someone' is often heard but is non-standard; ask takes two objects (someone + something).

**Principle:** ask someone something; or put a question to someone.

**Memory tip:** You ask the class a question - not 'ask a question to the class'.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Unnecessary, Wrong, Missing or Correct

questions.stem: State whether the preposition is unnecessary, missing, wrong, or correct - then fix if needed: 'I look forward your reply.'
questions.answer: Missing preposition. It should be 'look forward to your reply'. Corrected: 'I look forward to your reply.'
questions.solution:
**Answer:** Missing preposition. It should be 'look forward to your reply'. Corrected: 'I look forward to your reply.'

**Why the other options are wrong:** The 'to' in 'look forward to' is easily dropped; here it is followed by a noun ('your reply'), so no -ing is involved.

**Principle:** look forward to + a noun (or -ing).

**Memory tip:** You look forward TO something.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Unnecessary, Wrong, Missing or Correct

questions.stem: State whether the preposition is unnecessary, missing, wrong, or correct - then fix if needed: 'He is angry on me.'
questions.answer: Wrong preposition. 'angry on' should be 'angry with me' (or 'angry at me' in American English). Corrected: 'He is angry with me.'
questions.solution:
**Answer:** Wrong preposition. 'angry on' should be 'angry with me' (or 'angry at me' in American English). Corrected: 'He is angry with me.'

**Why the other options are wrong:** 'angry on' is a calque; a person takes 'with' (traditionally) or 'at' (American English), never 'on'.

**Principle:** angry with / at + a person (not 'on').

**Memory tip:** You're angry WITH a person, not 'on' them.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Unnecessary, Wrong, Missing or Correct

questions.stem: State whether there is a preposition error, and fix it if so: 'They accused him of stealing.'
questions.answer: Correct - no change needed. 'accuse someone of + (doing) something' is the standard combination.
questions.solution:
**Answer:** Correct - no change needed. 'accuse someone of + (doing) something' is the standard combination.

**Why the other options are wrong:** The trap is changing 'of' to 'for'; accuse takes 'of' (blame takes 'for').

**Principle:** accuse someone of + a wrong; blame someone for + a result.

**Memory tip:** accuse OF; blame FOR.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Unnecessary, Wrong, Missing or Correct

questions.stem: Which sentences contain a preposition error? Select ALL that apply.

**Explanation:** (a) 'good in cooking' should be 'good at cooking'. (c) 'discussed about' should be 'discussed' (no 'about').

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'interested in' and (d) 'fond of' are already correct, so selecting them would be a mistake.

**Principle:** good at + activity; discuss + object (no about); interested in; fond of.

**Memory tip:** good AT, discuss it directly; interested IN, fond OF.

questions.stem: State whether the preposition/structure is correct, and fix it if not: 'Can you explain me this sum?'

questions.solution:
**Answer:** Wrong structure. It should be 'explain this sum to me' (explain something to someone). Corrected: 'Can you explain this sum to me?'

**Why the other options are wrong:** 'explain me' treats explain like 'tell/give' (which allow 'me' directly); explain needs 'to' before the person.

**Principle:** explain something to someone (not 'explain me something').

**Memory tip:** explain the sum TO me.

questions.stem: State whether the preposition is unnecessary, missing, wrong, or correct - then fix if needed: 'The medicine had no effect to the patient.'
questions.answer: Wrong preposition. 'effect to' should be 'effect on' (have an effect on someone/something). Corrected: 'The medicine had no effect on the patient.'

**Why the other options are wrong:** By analogy with 'do something to', people write 'effect to'; the fixed phrase is 'an effect on'.

**Principle:** have an effect on + someone/something.

**Memory tip:** An effect works ON its target.

questions.stem: This sentence looks informal but is it actually wrong? Decide and explain: 'This is the book I told you about.'
questions.answer: Correct - no change needed. Ending with 'about' is perfectly acceptable here; the stiff alternative 'the book about which I told you' is not required in modern English.
questions.solution:
**Answer:** Correct - no change needed. Ending with 'about' is perfectly acceptable here; the stiff alternative 'the book about which I told you' is not required in modern English.

**Why the other options are wrong:** The trap is the myth that a sentence may never end with a preposition; here the preposition naturally falls at the end and the sentence is standard.

**Principle:** A sentence may end with a preposition when the phrasing is natural ('told you about').

**Memory tip:** 'Never end a sentence with a preposition' is a myth - this is fine.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Unnecessary, Wrong, Missing or Correct

questions.stem: In which sentence is the preposition used correctly?
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** 'keen on + noun/-ing' is correct. The others add an unnecessary preposition.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (a) 'married with' -\> married (to). (b) 'resembles to' -\> resembles. (d) 'reached to' -\> reached.

**Principle:** keen on + activity; marry someone; resemble someone; reach a place.

**Memory tip:** keen ON; but marry/resemble/reach take their object directly.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Unnecessary, Wrong, Missing or Correct

questions.stem: \_\_\_ the heavy rain, the match continued; \_\_\_ being tired, the players fought on.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** in spite of and despite mean the same, but despite takes NO 'of'.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'Despite of' is wrong, and 'In spite' without 'of' is incomplete. (c) 'Despite of' is wrong. (d) 'Although' is a conjunction and needs a clause ('although they were tired'), not a noun phrase.

**Principle:** in spite of + noun/gerund; despite + noun/gerund (no 'of'); although + a clause.

**Memory tip:** 'despite' already includes the 'of' meaning - never say 'despite of'.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Prepositional Phrases

questions.stem: Choose the traditionally correct option: 'The match was cancelled \_\_\_ the storm, and the cancellation was \_\_\_ safety concerns.'
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** Traditionally, 'because of' modifies the verb ('was cancelled because of the storm'), while 'due to' attaches to a noun through 'be' ('the cancellation was due to safety concerns'). Modern usage often blurs this.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) reversed: traditionally 'due to' should not modify the verb 'cancelled', and 'the cancellation was because of' is the looser half. (c) 'the cancellation was because of' is accepted in modern usage but not the crisp traditional pairing. (d) 'owing to' works like 'because of' (adverbial), leaving 'was because of' as the loose half.

**Principle:** Traditionally: 'due to' follows a noun/'be' (a delay due to fog); 'because of'/'owing to' modify a verb (delayed because of fog).

**Memory tip:** 'the X was due to...' (attaches to a noun); 'happened because of...' (attaches to a verb).
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Prepositional Phrases

fields.Cognitive skill: due to vs because of (traditional distinction)

questions.stem: \_\_\_ complaining, why not offer a solution? Later she chose tea \_\_\_ coffee.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** instead of + noun/gerund (complaining; coffee).

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'Instead complaining' drops 'of'. (c) 'In spite of complaining' changes the meaning. (d) 'instead coffee' drops 'of'. Note 'instead' alone is an adverb ('I'll have tea instead').

**Principle:** instead of + noun/gerund; instead (alone) = an adverb at the end.

**Memory tip:** Before a noun -\> 'instead of'; standing alone -\> 'instead'.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Prepositional Phrases

questions.stem: \_\_\_ the weather forecast, it will rain tomorrow.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** according to + a source.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'According' alone is incomplete. (c) 'As per to' is wrong ('as per' takes no 'to' and is jargon). (d) 'according with' is wrong.

**Principle:** according to + a source (but never 'according to me' - use 'in my opinion').

**Memory tip:** according TO a source; but 'in my opinion', never 'according to me'.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Prepositional Phrases

questions.stem: The head girl accepted the trophy \_\_\_ the whole school.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** on behalf of = representing / for someone.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'on behalf to' is wrong. (c) 'in behalf to' is wrong. (d) 'on the behalf' drops 'of'.

**Principle:** on behalf of + someone (representing them).

**Memory tip:** You act ON BEHALF OF the people you represent.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Prepositional Phrases

questions.stem: I am writing \_\_\_ your recent complaint.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** with regard to (singular 'regard') = concerning. 'regarding' and 'as regards' are also correct.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'with regards to' is non-standard - 'regards' (plural) is for greetings ('give my regards'). (c) 'in regards to' is non-standard. (d) 'with regard of' is wrong.

**Principle:** with regard to / in regard to / as regards / regarding; 'regards' only for greetings.

**Memory tip:** The linking phrase uses singular 'regard'; save 'regards' for 'best regards'.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Prepositional Phrases

questions.stem: \_\_\_ his salary, he earns money from tutoring.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** in addition to + noun/gerund.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'In addition' needs a comma + clause ('In addition, he earns...'), not a noun directly. (c) 'Additional to' is wrong. (d) 'In addition of' is wrong.

**Principle:** in addition to + noun/gerund; 'in addition' (alone) links clauses.

**Memory tip:** Before a noun -\> 'in addition to'; as a connector -\> 'in addition,'.

**Principle:** by means of + a method/instrument.

**Memory tip:** by MEANS of = by using.

questions.stem: Correct the form: 'Inspite of the traffic, we arrived on time.'

**Principle:** despite / in spite of + noun/gerund; although + clause.

**Memory tip:** 'Despite working' (no 'of'); 'although he worked'.

**Answer:** 'Inspite of' should be 'In spite of'; 'according with' should be 'according to'. Corrected: 'In spite of the delay, and according to the notice, refunds will be given to all passengers.'

questions.stem: Explain the difference: (i) 'He threw the ball to me.' (ii) 'He threw the ball at me.'
questions.answer: (i) to = he passed it for me to catch - I am the intended receiver (cooperative). (ii) at = he aimed it at me, usually to hit me (hostile/target). So 'to' = giving/passing; 'at' = aiming/attacking.
questions.solution:
**Answer:** (i) to = he passed it for me to catch - I am the intended receiver (cooperative). (ii) at = he aimed it at me, usually to hit me (hostile/target). So 'to' = giving/passing; 'at' = aiming/attacking.

**Why the other options are wrong:** Error: treating at and to as interchangeable after throw.

**Principle:** throw/pass to = the intended recipient; throw at = a target/aim (often hostile).

**Memory tip:** to = 'here, catch it'; at = 'take that!'.

questions.stem: Which word shows the thief was AIMING to hit the guard? 'The thief hurled a stone \_\_\_ the guard.'

**Explanation:** hurl/throw at = aim to strike.

questions.stem: Explain the difference: (i) 'The plane flew over the town.' (ii) 'The plane flew above the clouds.'
questions.answer: (i) over = across the top of the town, crossing from one side to the other. (ii) above = at a higher level than the clouds (a vertical relationship, simply 'higher than'). So 'over' suggests crossing/covering; 'above' suggests only 'higher than'.
questions.solution:
**Answer:** (i) over = across the top of the town, crossing from one side to the other. (ii) above = at a higher level than the clouds (a vertical relationship, simply 'higher than'). So 'over' suggests crossing/covering; 'above' suggests only 'higher than'.

**Why the other options are wrong:** Error: assuming over and above are identical.

**Principle:** over = across the top / crossing; above = at a higher level.

**Memory tip:** over = across it; above = higher than it.

questions.stem: Explain the difference: (i) 'She walked across the field.' (ii) 'She walked through the field.'
questions.answer: (i) across = from one side of the field to the other, over its open surface. (ii) through = among whatever fills the field (tall crops, long grass), moving amid it. 'Across' focuses on reaching the other side; 'through' focuses on passing among things in it.
questions.solution:
**Answer:** (i) across = from one side of the field to the other, over its open surface. (ii) through = among whatever fills the field (tall crops, long grass), moving amid it. 'Across' focuses on reaching the other side; 'through' focuses on passing among things in it.

**Why the other options are wrong:** Error: treating across and through as the same for a field.

**Principle:** across = over the surface, side to side; through = among what fills the space.

**Memory tip:** across = over the top; through = in among it.

questions.stem: Explain the difference (say if it is small): (i) 'I spoke to the manager.' (ii) 'I spoke with the manager.'
questions.answer: The difference is small. 'spoke with' slightly suggests a two-way conversation between equals; 'spoke to' can suggest a more one-directional exchange (you addressed them, perhaps to instruct). In most contexts they are interchangeable, with 'with' feeling a little more mutual.

**Why the other options are wrong:** Error: thinking one is wrong; both are correct.

**Principle:** speak to = address someone; speak with = converse with (more mutual); largely interchangeable.

**Memory tip:** 'with' hints at a two-way chat; 'to' can be one-way.

questions.stem: Explain the difference: (i) 'The letter was written by Gandhi.' (ii) 'The letter was written with a fountain pen.'
questions.answer: (i) by = the agent/author who performed the writing (Gandhi). (ii) with = the instrument/tool used to write (a fountain pen). So 'by' names who did the action; 'with' names what was used to do it.
questions.solution:
**Answer:** (i) by = the agent/author who performed the writing (Gandhi). (ii) with = the instrument/tool used to write (a fountain pen). So 'by' names who did the action; 'with' names what was used to do it.

**Why the other options are wrong:** Error: confusing the agent (by) with the instrument (with).

**Principle:** by + the doer (agent); with + the tool (instrument).

**Memory tip:** by = who did it; with = what they used.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Meaning Change Through Preposition Choice

questions.stem: Choose the option that names the TOOL used: 'The sculpture was carved \_\_\_ a chisel \_\_\_ a local artist.'
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** carved with a chisel (the tool) by a local artist (the agent).

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) reversed: 'carved by a chisel' wrongly makes the chisel the doer, and 'with a local artist' wrongly makes the artist a tool. (c)/(d) use one word for both, confusing tool and doer.

**Principle:** with + instrument; by + agent.

**Memory tip:** with the tool, by the person.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Meaning Change Through Preposition Choice

questions.stem: Explain the difference: (i) 'She sat by the window.' (ii) 'She sat near the window.'
questions.answer: (i) by = right beside / immediately next to the window. (ii) near = close to it but not necessarily right beside it - a little further away. So 'by' means directly alongside; 'near' means in the general area.
questions.solution:
**Answer:** (i) by = right beside / immediately next to the window. (ii) near = close to it but not necessarily right beside it - a little further away. So 'by' means directly alongside; 'near' means in the general area.

**Why the other options are wrong:** Error: treating by and near as identical distances.

**Principle:** by = immediately beside; near = in the vicinity (looser).

**Memory tip:** by = right at it; near = around there.

questions.stem: Explain the difference: (i) 'She ran into her old teacher at the market.' (ii) 'She ran to her old teacher at the market.'
questions.answer: (i) run into (someone) = meet by chance / unexpectedly (an idiom). (ii) run to (someone) = physically move quickly towards them, on purpose. So 'ran into' = happened to meet; 'ran to' = deliberately went over to them.
questions.solution:
**Answer:** (i) run into (someone) = meet by chance / unexpectedly (an idiom). (ii) run to (someone) = physically move quickly towards them, on purpose. So 'ran into' = happened to meet; 'ran to' = deliberately went over to them.

**Why the other options are wrong:** Error: reading 'ran into' literally as a collision, or missing the idiom.

**Principle:** run into someone = meet unexpectedly (idiom); run to someone = move quickly towards them.

**Memory tip:** 'ran into' = bumped into by chance; 'ran to' = dashed over on purpose.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Meaning Change Through Preposition Choice

questions.stem: Explain any difference: (i) 'a book about science' (ii) 'a book on science'.
questions.answer: The difference is slight. 'a book on science' often suggests a more formal, academic or specialist treatment; 'a book about science' sounds a little more general or informal. In many cases they are interchangeable, with 'on' leaning scholarly and 'about' leaning general.
questions.solution:
**Answer:** The difference is slight. 'a book on science' often suggests a more formal, academic or specialist treatment; 'a book about science' sounds a little more general or informal. In many cases they are interchangeable, with 'on' leaning scholarly and 'about' leaning general.

**Why the other options are wrong:** Error: assuming they are always identical or always different.

**Principle:** on + subject (often scholarly/specialist); about + subject (often general); largely interchangeable.

**Memory tip:** 'on' feels like a textbook; 'about' feels like a general read.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Meaning Change Through Preposition Choice

questions.stem: Explain the difference: (i) 'She cares about her students.' (ii) 'She cares for her students.'
questions.answer: (i) care about = be concerned about / consider important (their wellbeing matters to her). (ii) care for = look after / tend to them (provide care), and in some contexts 'be fond of'. So 'care about' = emotional concern; 'care for' = looking after.
questions.solution:
**Answer:** (i) care about = be concerned about / consider important (their wellbeing matters to her). (ii) care for = look after / tend to them (provide care), and in some contexts 'be fond of'. So 'care about' = emotional concern; 'care for' = looking after.

**Why the other options are wrong:** Error: treating care about and care for as identical.

**Principle:** care about = be concerned about; care for = look after (or, in negatives/questions, like).

**Memory tip:** care ABOUT = it matters to me; care FOR = I tend to / look after.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Meaning Change Through Preposition Choice

questions.stem: Which shows that the nurse LOOKS AFTER the patients? 'The nurse cares \_\_\_ the patients day and night.'
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** care for = look after / tend to.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'cares about' = is concerned about (not the physical looking-after sense). (c) 'cares of' is wrong. (d) 'cares with' is wrong.

**Principle:** care for = look after.

**Memory tip:** care FOR = tend to.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Meaning Change Through Preposition Choice

questions.stem: Explain any difference: (i) 'I dream of becoming a pilot.' (ii) 'I dreamt about flying last night.'
questions.answer: (i) dream of = long for / aspire to (a waking ambition). (ii) dream about = have a dream (while asleep) featuring something. So 'dream of' usually means a hope or ambition; 'dream about' usually means the images you saw while sleeping. (They can overlap, but this is the typical split.)
questions.solution:
**Answer:** (i) dream of = long for / aspire to (a waking ambition). (ii) dream about = have a dream (while asleep) featuring something. So 'dream of' usually means a hope or ambition; 'dream about' usually means the images you saw while sleeping. (They can overlap, but this is the typical split.)

**Why the other options are wrong:** Error: mixing the ambition sense with the sleeping-dream sense.

**Principle:** dream of = aspire to; dream about = have a (sleeping) dream featuring.

**Memory tip:** dream OF = your ambition; dream ABOUT = last night's dream.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Meaning Change Through Preposition Choice

questions.stem: Explain the difference: (i) 'What do you think of my plan?' (ii) 'I need to think about your plan.'
questions.answer: (i) think of = have an opinion about (What is your opinion?). (ii) think about = consider / reflect on (spend time weighing it up). So 'think of' asks for an opinion; 'think about' means to ponder or consider.
questions.solution:
**Answer:** (i) think of = have an opinion about (What is your opinion?). (ii) think about = consider / reflect on (spend time weighing it up). So 'think of' asks for an opinion; 'think about' means to ponder or consider.

**Why the other options are wrong:** Error: treating think of and think about as identical.

**Principle:** think of = have an opinion (or bring to mind); think about = consider / ponder.

**Memory tip:** think OF = your verdict; think ABOUT = mull it over.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Meaning Change Through Preposition Choice

questions.stem: Explain the difference between: (i) 'Did you hear the news?' (ii) 'Have you heard of this band?' (iii) 'Have you heard from your sister?'
questions.answer: (i) hear = perceive a sound / receive information (the news reached you). (ii) hear of = know that something or someone exists (be aware of the band). (iii) hear from = receive a message or contact from someone (your sister contacted you). The particle changes the meaning from 'perceive' to 'know of the existence' to 'be contacted by'.
questions.solution:
**Answer:** (i) hear = perceive a sound / receive information (the news reached you). (ii) hear of = know that something or someone exists (be aware of the band). (iii) hear from = receive a message or contact from someone (your sister contacted you). The particle changes the meaning from 'perceive' to 'know of the existence' to 'be contacted by'.

**Why the other options are wrong:** Error: mixing 'hear of' (know it exists) with 'hear from' (be contacted).

**Principle:** hear = perceive; hear of = know of the existence; hear from = be contacted by.

**Memory tip:** hear it; hear OF it (know it exists); hear FROM someone (they contact you).
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Meaning Change Through Preposition Choice

questions.stem: Explain the difference: (i) 'The flood resulted in huge damage.' (ii) 'The damage resulted from the flood.'
questions.answer: (i) result in = lead to / cause (the flood is the cause, the damage the effect). (ii) result from = be caused by (the damage is the effect, the flood the cause). The two reverse the cause-effect order: 'result in' points to the effect; 'result from' points to the cause.
questions.solution:
**Answer:** (i) result in = lead to / cause (the flood is the cause, the damage the effect). (ii) result from = be caused by (the damage is the effect, the flood the cause). The two reverse the cause-effect order: 'result in' points to the effect; 'result from' points to the cause.

**Why the other options are wrong:** Error: swapping the direction of cause and effect.

**Principle:** X results in Y = X causes Y; Y results from X = Y is caused by X.

**Memory tip:** result IN the effect; result FROM the cause.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Meaning Change Through Preposition Choice

questions.stem: Which preposition makes the sentence mean the delay CAUSED the loss? 'The heavy loss resulted \_\_\_ the long delay.'
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** 'the loss resulted from the delay' = the delay caused the loss (the loss is the effect, the delay the cause).

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'resulted in the delay' would mean the loss caused the delay (reversed). (c) 'resulted of' is wrong. (d) 'resulted to' is wrong.

**Principle:** the effect + results from + the cause.

**Memory tip:** The effect results FROM the cause.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Meaning Change Through Preposition Choice

questions.stem: Explain the difference: (i) 'The teacher talked to the students.' (ii) 'The teacher talked at the students.'
questions.answer: (i) talk to = address them in a normal, two-way or considerate way. (ii) talk at = speak in their direction without engaging or letting them respond (one-sided, often hectoring). So 'talk to' is communicative; 'talk at' ignores the listener.
questions.solution:
**Answer:** (i) talk to = address them in a normal, two-way or considerate way. (ii) talk at = speak in their direction without engaging or letting them respond (one-sided, often hectoring). So 'talk to' is communicative; 'talk at' ignores the listener.

**Why the other options are wrong:** Error: missing that 'at' here signals a lack of real engagement.

**Principle:** talk to = communicate with; talk at = speak without engaging (one-sided).

**Memory tip:** talk TO = a real exchange; talk AT = you're just a wall they speak toward.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Meaning Change Through Preposition Choice

questions.stem: Explain the difference: (i) 'He shouted at the boy.' (ii) 'He shouted to the boy.'
questions.answer: (i) shout at = shout angrily/aggressively towards someone (hostile). (ii) shout to = call out loudly so they can hear (e.g. across a distance), not necessarily angry. So 'at' = angry; 'to' = calling to be heard.
questions.solution:
**Answer:** (i) shout at = shout angrily/aggressively towards someone (hostile). (ii) shout to = call out loudly so they can hear (e.g. across a distance), not necessarily angry. So 'at' = angry; 'to' = calling to be heard.

**Why the other options are wrong:** Error: assuming both mean anger.

**Principle:** shout at = angrily; shout to = to be heard across a distance.

**Memory tip:** shout AT = telling off; shout TO = calling out.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Meaning Change Through Preposition Choice

questions.stem: Explain the difference: (i) 'The team consists of eleven players.' (ii) 'True happiness consists in contentment.'
questions.answer: (i) consist of = be made up of (parts or members). (ii) consist in = have its essential nature in / be based on (a more abstract, formal use). So 'consist of' lists the components; 'consist in' identifies what something essentially is.
questions.solution:
**Answer:** (i) consist of = be made up of (parts or members). (ii) consist in = have its essential nature in / be based on (a more abstract, formal use). So 'consist of' lists the components; 'consist in' identifies what something essentially is.

**Why the other options are wrong:** Error: not knowing 'consist in' exists, or using 'consist of' where the meaning is 'lies in / is based on'.

**Principle:** consist of = be composed of (parts); consist in = have its essence in.

**Memory tip:** consist OF = the ingredients; consist IN = the essence.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Meaning Change Through Preposition Choice

questions.stem: Which sentence means the author PERSONALLY contacted you?
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** hear from = receive contact / a message from someone.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (a) heard = perceived a sound. (b) heard of = know the author exists. (d) heard about = learned information concerning the author (from someone else), not direct contact.

**Principle:** hear from = be contacted by (a direct message).

**Memory tip:** hear FROM = they reached out to you.

questions.stem: We usually travel \_\_\_ train, but yesterday we went \_\_\_ car.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** by + a means of transport (no article) states the general method: by train, by car, by bus, by plane (but 'on foot').

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b)/(c)/(d) mix 'on'/'in'. You may say 'in the car' or 'on the train' about a specific vehicle, but the general method is 'by car', 'by train'; both blanks want the general method.

**Principle:** by + means of transport (no article) for the general method: by car/bus/train/plane; on foot.

**Memory tip:** How did you travel? -\> by car/train/bus (but 'on foot').
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Abstract and Non-Physical Prepositions

questions.stem: He earns a living \_\_\_ teaching, and he marks the essays \_\_\_ a red pen.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** by + gerund states the method (by teaching); with + an instrument states the tool (with a red pen).

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'with teaching' is wrong (method needs by + -ing), and 'by a red pen' wrongly makes the pen the doer. (c) 'by a red pen' makes the pen the doer. (d) 'with teaching' is wrong.

**Principle:** by + gerund (method: by teaching); with + instrument (with a pen); never 'by a pen'.

**Memory tip:** You earn a living BY doing something; you write WITH a tool.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Abstract and Non-Physical Prepositions

questions.stem: Explain the usual difference: (i) 'She died of cancer.' (ii) 'He died from his injuries.'
questions.answer: The traditional split is: 'die of' + an illness or internal condition (cancer, a fever, old age, hunger); 'die from' + an external cause or injury (wounds, a fall, exposure). In practice the two overlap and both are often accepted, but this is the usual guideline.
questions.solution:
**Answer:** The traditional split is: 'die of' + an illness or internal condition (cancer, a fever, old age, hunger); 'die from' + an external cause or injury (wounds, a fall, exposure). In practice the two overlap and both are often accepted, but this is the usual guideline.

**Why the other options are wrong:** Error: using 'die by' for a disease - 'die by' is for a method of death ('die by drowning').

**Principle:** die of + an illness/condition; die from + an injury/external cause; die by + a method.

**Memory tip:** of an illness, from a wound, by a method.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Abstract and Non-Physical Prepositions

questions.stem: Half the class voted \_\_\_ the school trip, while the other half voted \_\_\_ it.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** vote for = in support of; vote against = in opposition to.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'voted to the trip' is wrong. (c) 'versus' is not used after 'voted' like this. (d) 'voted with' means 'voted the same way as (a person)', not 'in support of the trip'.

**Principle:** for = in support of; against = in opposition to.

**Memory tip:** FOR = yes/support; AGAINST = no/oppose.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Abstract and Non-Physical Prepositions

questions.stem: All the players trained hard \_\_\_ the goalkeeper, who was injured; and \_\_\_ training, they also studied match videos.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** except (the goalkeeper) = not including him; besides (training) = in addition to training.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) swapped: 'besides the goalkeeper' = in addition to him (but he is excluded); 'except training' = excluding training (but it is additional). (c) 'beside training' = physically next to training. (d) loses the 'excluding' meaning.

**Principle:** except (for) = not including; besides = in addition to.

**Memory tip:** except = leave out; besides = add on.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Abstract and Non-Physical Prepositions

questions.stem: This drink is made \_\_\_ real oranges, and the smell \_\_\_ oranges filled the room.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** made from real oranges (the source is transformed into juice); the smell of oranges (of = the characteristic quality belonging to oranges).

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'made of oranges' understates the transformation (the juice no longer looks like oranges), and 'the smell from oranges' is less idiomatic than 'the smell of'. (c) 'the smell from oranges' is less idiomatic. (d) 'made of oranges' understates the transformation.

**Principle:** made from (a transformed source); the smell/taste of X (a quality of X).

**Memory tip:** made FROM the source; the smell OF the thing.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Abstract and Non-Physical Prepositions

questions.stem: Scientists found a clear connection \_\_\_ smoking and lung disease.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** a connection/link/difference between X and Y - two items joined by 'and'.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'among' needs a group of three or more, not two named items joined by 'and'. (c) 'connection with smoking and lung disease' - the correct frame for two linked items is 'between ... and'. (d) 'connection of' is wrong.

**Principle:** a connection/link/difference between X and Y (two items); connection with/to (a single other thing).

**Memory tip:** between two named things joined by 'and'.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Abstract and Non-Physical Prepositions

questions.stem: The committee published a report \_\_\_ road safety, and a child wrote a story \_\_\_ a magic train.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** a report on road safety ('report on' is the established phrase for a factual document); a story about a magic train (about = concerning).

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'a report about' is weaker/informal, and 'a story on a magic train' is wrong. (c) 'a story on a magic train' is wrong. (d) 'a report about road safety' is weaker than the standard 'report on'.

**Principle:** report on / lecture on / book on = the established topic phrase (esp. factual/academic); story/novel/film about = concerning.

**Memory tip:** Factual works are 'on' a topic; stories are 'about' something.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Abstract and Non-Physical Prepositions

questions.stem: I found this flat \_\_\_ a friend who works at an agency.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** through + an intermediary = by means of / via someone acting as a channel (the friend helped you find it).

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'by a friend' would suggest the friend did the finding (the agent). (c) 'from a friend' = the flat came from the friend (e.g. they gave it to you). (d) 'with a friend' = together with the friend.

**Principle:** through + an intermediary/channel = by means of (via someone/something).

**Memory tip:** through a friend = your friend was the channel.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Abstract and Non-Physical Prepositions

questions.stem: She returned the wallet \_\_\_ honesty, not \_\_\_ fear of being caught.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** out of + a motive/feeling (honesty; fear) = because of that feeling.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'from honesty'/'of fear' - the motive phrase is 'out of'. (c) 'in fear' means 'in a state of fear', a different nuance, so mixing is inconsistent. (d) 'of honesty' is wrong.

**Principle:** out of + a motive/feeling (out of kindness, fear, curiosity, respect) = because of it.

**Memory tip:** 'out of X' = driven by X (the motive).
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Abstract and Non-Physical Prepositions

questions.stem: The bridge is currently \_\_\_ construction, and the cause of the collapse is \_\_\_ investigation.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** under + certain nouns = in the process of / subject to: under construction, under investigation.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'in construction' is wrong (it is 'under construction'). (c)/(d) mix 'on'/'in' where 'under' is required.

**Principle:** under + certain nouns = in the process of: under construction, investigation, discussion, review, repair, control.

**Memory tip:** 'under construction' = being built; 'under investigation' = being looked into.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Abstract and Non-Physical Prepositions

questions.stem: The instructions were \_\_\_ my understanding, and the noise was \_\_\_ belief.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** beyond + an abstract limit = past what is possible: beyond my understanding, beyond belief.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'above my understanding' is sometimes heard, but 'beyond' is the standard idiom ('beyond me'); 'beyond belief' is fixed. (c)/(d) 'over/above belief' are wrong.

**Principle:** beyond + an abstract limit: beyond belief, beyond repair, beyond doubt, beyond my understanding.

**Memory tip:** 'beyond belief' = too much to believe.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Abstract and Non-Physical Prepositions

questions.stem: State whether there is a preposition error, and fix it if so: 'She was trembling with fear and could not speak because of nervousness.'
questions.answer: Correct - no change needed. 'trembling with fear' (the emotion causing the physical reaction) and 'because of nervousness' (the reason) are both right.
questions.solution:
**Answer:** Correct - no change needed. 'trembling with fear' (the emotion causing the physical reaction) and 'because of nervousness' (the reason) are both right.

**Why the other options are wrong:** The trap is 'correcting' a sentence that is already right - for example changing 'with fear' to 'from/of fear', or 'because of' to 'due to' unnecessarily.

**Principle:** with + an emotion causing a reaction (tremble with fear); because of + a reason.

**Memory tip:** You tremble WITH fear; you stop BECAUSE OF nervousness.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Abstract and Non-Physical Prepositions

questions.stem: He was shaking \_\_\_ anger and his face was red \_\_\_ embarrassment.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** with + an emotion = the emotion causing a physical reaction (shaking with anger, red with embarrassment).

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'shaking of anger' is wrong. (c) 'shaking from anger' is heard, but 'with' is the standard for an emotion-driven reaction. (d) 'shaking by anger' is wrong.

**Principle:** with + emotion = the emotion causing a physical state (tremble with fear, shake with anger, red with embarrassment).

**Memory tip:** shaking WITH anger = anger makes you shake.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Abstract and Non-Physical Prepositions

questions.stem: She takes vitamins \_\_\_ her health and wears a helmet \_\_\_ injury.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** for her health = purpose/benefit; against injury = protection/guarding from.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'a helmet for injury' would wrongly suggest the helmet is meant to cause injury; protection takes 'against'. (c) 'to her health' is wrong. (d) 'vitamins against her health' reverses the sense.

**Principle:** for = purpose/benefit; against = protection / guarding from.

**Memory tip:** FOR a benefit; AGAINST a danger.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Abstract and Non-Physical Prepositions

questions.stem: Explain the difference: (i) 'I'm afraid of my dog.' (ii) 'I'm afraid for my dog.'
questions.answer: (i) afraid of = frightened by the dog (the dog is the threat to me). (ii) afraid for = worried about the dog's safety (the dog is in danger and I fear on its behalf). So 'of' = the source of my fear; 'for' = the one I fear on behalf of.
questions.solution:
**Answer:** (i) afraid of = frightened by the dog (the dog is the threat to me). (ii) afraid for = worried about the dog's safety (the dog is in danger and I fear on its behalf). So 'of' = the source of my fear; 'for' = the one I fear on behalf of.

**Why the other options are wrong:** Error: treating of and for as identical after afraid.

**Principle:** afraid of = scared by something; afraid for = worried about someone's safety.

**Memory tip:** afraid OF the threat; afraid FOR the one at risk.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Abstract and Non-Physical Prepositions

questions.stem: The country was \_\_\_ chaos, the soldiers stood \_\_\_ silence, and the plan lay \_\_\_ ruins.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** in + an abstract state/condition: in chaos, in silence, in ruins.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b)/(c)/(d) mix 'on'/'at', which are wrong for these fixed 'in + state' phrases.

**Principle:** in + a state/condition: in chaos, in silence, in ruins, in danger, in love, in trouble, in doubt.

**Memory tip:** A state or condition takes 'in'.
topics: Grammar > Prepositions > Abstract and Non-Physical Prepositions

questions.stem: She was thrilled \_\_\_ the good news but alarmed \_\_\_ the sudden change of plan.
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** at + a trigger of an emotional reaction (thrilled at, alarmed at); 'by' is also acceptable, but 'on' is not.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b)/(c)/(d) use 'on'/'with' where 'at' expresses the reaction; 'thrilled on' and 'alarmed on' are wrong.

**Principle:** at (or by) + a trigger of a reaction: surprised/shocked/alarmed/delighted/thrilled at.

**Memory tip:** You react AT (or by) a piece of news.

questions.stem: Choose the best set: 'She kept calm \_\_\_ the crisis, acted \_\_\_ the interest of everyone, and stayed \_\_\_ control throughout.'
questions.solution:
**Explanation:** during the crisis (throughout the event); in the interest of everyone (fixed phrase); in control = remained in charge.

**Why the other options are wrong:** (b) 'in the crisis' is weaker, 'on the interest' is wrong, and 'stayed under control' would mean she was being kept in check (wrong - she stayed in charge). (c) 'on the interest' is wrong. (d) 'at the crisis' is wrong.

**Principle:** during + an event; in the interest(s) of (fixed); in control = in charge (vs under control = being managed).

**Memory tip:** during the crisis; in everyone's interest; she stayed in control (in charge).
